whatItFakes: Drive acts (tell someone, join, donate, volunteer, confront, seek standing) with prototype durations and consequences; outcomes beyond money, membership and relationships are not modeled.
why: Drives must move people, money and relationships inside the core; full group and civic procedures do not exist yet.
replacement: Group, charity and civic engines whose procedures decide outcomes, with durations from ATUS.

whatItFakes: A resident founds a cause group instantly with no charter, registration, dues or officers.
why: Organizing needs a place for others to join; the nonprofit and association engine is not built.
replacement: An association engine with formation steps, registration law per place and membership rules.

whatItFakes: Testifying at a hearing is a registered act row that is never offered.
why: Core2 has no hearings or legislature.
replacement: Resolved Oct 19: the act row is deleted. Testimony is a resident's remark at a hearing or meeting (the meetings module's remarks and hearings), chosen from the resident's own views, so a second drive act would be a parallel route.

whatItFakes: Running for office is a registered act row that is never offered.
why: Core2 has no elections or filing.
replacement: Resolved Oct 19: the act row is deleted. Who runs is decided by the elections and candidacy modules (candidacy.ts, candidate-pool.ts, world-races), so a drive act would be a parallel route.

whatItFakes: Lobbying a legislator is a registered act row that is never offered.
why: Core2 has no legislature or member contact system.
replacement: Resolved Oct 19: the act row is deleted. Lobbying is the interest-groups module's contact with a legislator, so a drive act would be a parallel route.

whatItFakes: Only the opening chronic conditions, the serious-illness onset and the death of the Ruling 29/38/39 mortality rule run in core2; conditions beginning during life, coverage, poverty onset causes, injuries and births are absent.
why: P10 needs a real recorded death from illness; no core2 health engine exists.
replacement: A full core2 health engine ported per the P11 plan.

whatItFakes: Event impulses scale Holmes-Rahe life change units into core2 stress and mood impulses with tunable conversions.
why: Events need a sized emotional impact; the life-change ranking is sourced but its conversion to the affect scale is not.
replacement: A calibrated appraisal model checked against bereavement and illness affect trajectories.

whatItFakes: One base-rate scale (0.106) for every place, solved from two generated towns so expected yearly deaths match the SSA 2023 life table; the chronic-condition weights were calibrated for the old shared threshold and are not refit.
why: The owner replaced the shared threshold with personal resilience lines; totals must stay on the life table and a full recalibration of the condition pack has not been done.
replacement: A cohort calibration of base scale and condition weights together, checked across many places and ages against the life table.

whatItFakes: A founded cause group carries a structured key in its name field instead of a name.
why: Names must come from the English engine; no naming bank for groups exists in core2.
replacement: An English-engine naming bank for associations reading topic and place.

whatItFakes: How fast outlets reach people by how closely they follow politics, how long a story stays news, and how many stories pass at a contact; one generic local outlet stands for all.
why: Basic news (M2-09) needs a first version before outlets and media habits are modeled.
replacement: Named local outlets with real audiences and each person's recorded media habits (Pew local news surveys), checked against how fast election results spread.

whatItFakes: How much a speech moves listeners and who retells it; retelling reaches only the listener's household.
why: Speeches (M4-04) need a first reception model; persuasion research gives directions and small averages, not these coefficients.
replacement: Reception calibrated to persuasion experiments by audience and message (Coppock 2023), retelling through friends and the news module, and memory by age (M4-04).

whatItFakes: How much traits, money pressure and ties weigh in offering, taking and telling about a bribe.
why: Basic corruption (M3-09) needs a first version; the research gives directions, not these coefficients.
replacement: Weights checked against bribery incidence surveys and public-corruption case counts by office (DOJ Public Integrity Section reports), with audits and the news surfacing records.

whatItFakes: Each adult's education and faith at the opening, read from their state's CES 2024 shares by age band with a household share; education and faith are treated as independent within a state and age band, and children carry no attainment.
why: Views and candidacy need education and faith on records now; joint state tables are too sparse in one survey year.
replacement: Attainment from the person's own schooling history (deep past) checked against ACS B15001 by state, age and sex; faith from upbringing and the Pew Religious Landscape Study.

whatItFakes: Opening 30-year mortgage rates after April 2019 are the 10-year Treasury plus the 1990-2019 mean FHFA spread, not a published monthly rate.
why: FHFA's monthly survey ended in 2019; public HMDA is annual and Freddie Mac's survey is excluded (CTO ruling on #3959).
replacement: A government monthly mortgage-rate series, or monthly HMDA origination dates if CFPB publishes them.

whatItFakes: State and local budgets add no impulse to national output beyond their real average, and neither does the federal budget in a world without the budgets engine. Where the budgets engine runs, the federal budget's change from its base is read each month through macroFiscalMultiplier (Oct 14, OPUS-WORLD).
why: Other states' and towns' budgets are not kept in the world, and one town's own budgets are too small a share of the nation to move it.
replacement: Resolved Oct 16 (owner ruling, no fiscal multiplier): the macro engine carries no budget impulse or multiplier. A public dollar moves output through who is paid and what they spend, read by the budgets, regional and jobs engines; the research ranges stay as a check on the totals.

whatItFakes: When a counted household with an open eviction case is filled in, the case follows the household and its lease takes up the arrears the group had run up at notice, from the notice date. Whether the arrears carry over, are cured by the fill-in, or the case closes is the owner's call.
why: A counted household is not a second simulation: filled in, it must be the same household with the same debt (one model, two tiers). No ruling exists on its arrears.
replacement: The owner's ruling on carry, cure or close for a counted household's arrears on fill-in (docs/coordination/OWNER-DECISIONS.md).
resolution: Whether a filled-in household carries arrears depends on the people: a filled-in household carries its group's arrears onto its own lease, then settles part of them at once from the cash its members hold beyond a month of living cost times how far their traits lean toward settling over letting it lapse (the formula decision housing.settle-arrears); what it does not settle stays on the lease for the cure deadline. The case records the cash, living cost, willingness and sum settled.

whatItFakes: A seat's new member is the seeded candidate whose lived inflation sits closest to the board's middle, chosen without the president or the Senate.
why: OPUS-GOV's nominateAndConfirm (the president's side picks, the real Senate confirms) is on its branch, not yet on this one.
replacement: registerBoardAppointer with nominateAndConfirm once the offices and appointments modules are on the same branch. Done Oct 15 (board-appointer.ts, registered by openSuccession): a governor is named by the president and confirmed by the Senate; a reserve bank president is chosen and approved by the sitting governors. Open rows it brings: SG-WORLD-board-hawk-side and SG-WORLD-board-career-qualification.

whatItFakes: One named business gets a prime-linked credit line from a town lender for the M1-02 proof; no bank chose to lend.
why: The generated opening has no credit lines; banks and loans are M1-06 (OPUS-WORLD, next on the checklist).
replacement: M1-06 credit: banks that lend from their own books and the borrower's record, with lines indexed to prime.
resolvedBy: Second Session D, October 15, 2026: removed the obsolete stand-in writer and changed macro-proof to buildBenchWorld; credit.ts supplies bank applications and prime-linked facilities from the bank and borrower books.

whatItFakes: Guam, American Samoa, the Northern Marianas and the Virgin Islands start from their own latest published unemployment rate held flat (src/core2/data/regional/territories.json; American Samoa from the 2020 Census, the Marianas from a 2017 survey), with the nation's pay and price level and no industry mix.
why: They are outside the CBSA, CBP, LAUS and BEA tables in the repo; their governments' labor statistics are not yet gathered.
replacement: Each territory's own published labor and price statistics (Guam BLS-funded surveys, USVI Bureau of Economic Research, CNMI and American Samoa statistical offices), or the nearest comparable economy, labeled with its source.

whatItFakes: The opening's job seekers are the jobless working-age adults whose money covers the fewest days, as many as the nation's unemployment rate implies against the generated jobs; the other jobless adults sit outside the modeled labor market.
why: The generated opening employs only part of the town (unsupported workplaces are omitted), so most jobless adults are not really unemployed; the two-level population (OPUS-CORE) will hold the rest as counts.
replacement: The two-level population's labor-force counts by place, age and job (CPS and LAUS), with full people filled in from them.
resolution: The opening's seekers are chosen per place from that place's own unemployment rate (the region's month when the regional engine runs, the nation's otherwise), for the named people and the counted ones alike.

whatItFakes: A layoff names the business itself as who decided it.
why: Businesses have no recorded owners or managers until businesses growing (M1-08). Resolved Oct 19, 2026: a layoff is decided by the recorded owner, else by the firm's best-paid full worker still on the staff (managerOf in modules/jobs.ts); only a firm with no one left decides as itself.
replacement: The owner or manager person recorded by M1-08, deciding from their own traits and the books.

whatItFakes: Every state's unemployment insurance pays half the lost weekly pay up to $611 a week for 26 weeks after one waiting week, with a $2,775 base-period minimum (the states' medians).
why: Resolved by OPUS-GOV (2026-10-14): jobs-benefits.ts reads lawInForce directly, no stand-in. Was: each state's own terms are law in force on OPUS-GOV's branch (lawInForce(api, "unemployment-insurance")), not yet on this one.
replacement: registerUnemploymentTerms with the state's terms from lawInForce once the laws module is on the same branch.

whatItFakes: A business with no recorded owner (a public employer, an ownerless landlord) applies for a line whenever its cash is below a few months of payroll; owned businesses' owners decide.
why: Businesses have no recorded owners until businesses growing (M1-08). Resolved Oct 19, 2026: a firm with no recorded owner is run by its best-paid full worker, who weighs the same reasons as an owner; with no full person, its counted people's summed pulls decide (modules/credit.ts).
replacement: Those organizations' own deciders (a board, a public budget) choose whether to borrow.

whatItFakes: The town bank opens holding only its own equity as cash and lends from that; households' and businesses' money is not on deposit with it.
why: Deposits need the core's named accounts (OPUS-CORE's accounts item) so cash can sit in bank accounts without a second book.
replacement: Session B: real household and business savings move to the bank through accounts/postJournal; lending reads cash and liabilities. Limited payment-path withdrawal coverage is tracked separately as SG-WORLD-deposit-wallet-buffer.

whatItFakes: All of a town's rentals belong to one landlord business with no owner; it serves notice by summed pulls of months owed and months late (calibrated to landlords filing at about two months owed), not by an owner's own patience and cash.
why: Landlords as businesses with owners who decide from their own books and patience come with businesses growing (M1-08).
replacement: Rentals owned by the town's own landlords (owners of rental businesses and individual owners), each deciding from their traits, cash and the tenant's history.

whatItFakes: Eviction steps not yet read from official text: of 56 places, 30 have the notice period read, 23 whether a tenant can cure, 36 the hearing period and 34 the stay; the other values are recalled from secondary summaries, and missing values take the median of the better-sourced places.
why: Three research passes read official code and court-rule sites; some sites refused or are Lexis-only (CA, CT, IL, UT, NJ, NM, GU, AL, AR, GA, MS, TN, IN, VI, AS). Per-place verifiedFields, hearingStaySources and verificationFailed are in data/research/housing/eviction-steps-2026.json.
replacement: Each place's steps read from the official statute text and cited by section, then M1-laws' landlord-tenant law in force.

whatItFakes: An eviction hearing ends in judgment whenever rent is still owed and notice was given, with no judge's discretion, defenses or counsel.
why: Courts are parked until after early access (owner, Oct 10). Resolved Oct 19 by the owner's Oct 14 ruling, 'Evictions without courts: an eviction completes after the state's notice period from the law in force; the household moves as the housing engine moves leavers. No court scene until courts come' (docs/coordination/OWNER-DECISIONS.md, DECISION-REGISTER.md). The hearing step is a dated step of the statute with no judge or scene, which is what the ruling asks for; the courts port is separate work.
replacement: The courts port: a judge deciding from the record, the tenant's defenses and any right to counsel in the law in force.

whatItFakes: The opening's largest businesses (by staff, up to the state's estimated share of jobs in multi-establishment firms) belong to firms based outside the town; every other is owned by its highest-paid current worker, as owner-operator.
why: The generated opening records no owners; founding by choice (this work order's next piece) gives new businesses their real founders.
replacement: Owners from the opening's history (who founded or bought each business, M1-14), with absentee and corporate owners from business ownership records.

whatItFakes: Completed rentals now admit unassigned households in either tier once income and cash qualify, and consume an actual vacancy. Existing-stock arrivals and departures still lack unit-level assignment.
why: New-unit occupancy and its vacancy changes are recorded; the opening rental stock has no individual unit inventory.
replacement: Record opening rental units and route their arrivals and departures through the same assignment and release rules.

whatItFakes: Counted workers (the wider population) retire, quit, start looking and stop looking by summed pulls (strongestPulls) rather than the shared chooser; they apply to every opening in their place, and an employed counted worker accepts by acceptScore. Counted closures and layoffs also run through this path.
why: The shared chooser needs a full person; filling in everyone who makes a job decision would undo the two-level population.
replacement: Fill-in at the moment a counted person meets an employer (OPUS-CORE's fillInPerson), or an aggregate chooser for counted groups agreed with OPUS-CORE.

whatItFakes: The wider population's renters pay rent from their place's pooled residents account, and the arrears they run up are held per group (households of one kind in one place), not per household; a case is opened and a household removed from the group's pool, but which household in the group is behind is not recorded.
why: The two-level population pools counted households' cash by place (OPUS-CORE's stopgap), so the group falls behind together; a single counted household's own shortfall is not kept.
replacement: Per-household cash for counted households (or fill-in when a household falls behind), with arrears and eviction through the same legal steps.

whatItFakes: A job that a saved visitor agreement names as its provider's qualification is never ended by a layoff, a quit, a retirement or a move to another job.
why: The core rejects the agreement's next payment once the named job ends ("Visitor qualification no longer resolves its actual product job"), seen in year two of Absecon, New Jersey.
replacement: OPUS-CORE lets a visitor agreement re-resolve its qualification to any current qualified worker at the provider; then this filter goes.
resolvedBy: Claude session on the pool item world-agreements-re-resolve-worker, October 19, 2026: deleted src/core2/pinned-jobs.ts and the jobs engine's filters on it. A saved agreement already follows its product jobs' real life in finance-cash.ts (productJobRelations: an ended job drops out and the supplier's current staff in the product occupations carry it; with none, the agreement ends), so a named job's holder may now be laid off, quit, retire or move.

whatItFakes: An owner still in the wider population (not yet filled in) takes the option whose reasons sum highest instead of choosing through the shared chooser, and their draws go to their place's pooled residents account.
why: Filling in every owner as a full person made a game year about 40% slower (Absecon, New Jersey); owners are filled in when the player meets them.
replacement: The shared chooser for counted people (the same reasons, without a full person), or full owners once a full person costs the core little per day.
resolvedBy: Second Session D, October 15, 2026: the shared chooser reads counted owners through the same initial actor shape without admitting them. Draws and closure proceeds reach the recorded owner household group; full owners keep their own accounts.

whatItFakes: Each owner's purchase year comes from the national move-in distribution by age rank, the purchase price is today's value moved back by the state's FHFA house price index, the loan is a 30-year fixed with the NAR median down payment and no refinancing, and the same county mortgage shares by age apply everywhere.
why: No house price index, county move-in or mortgage-balance table is in the data yet.
replacement: FHFA house price index by state and metro for purchase prices, ACS B25038 and B25027 by county, and refinancing waves from the rate history.

whatItFakes: Home prices follow FHFA's state house price index through its latest quarter (2026 Q2); after it, and where FHFA has no rows (Puerto Rico and the island areas), they follow consumer prices (CPI-U, which in the data ends in 2025). The seller in a purchase is outside the town.
why: FHFA publishes no index for Puerto Rico or the island areas, the simulated future has no house price model yet, and people don't move in or out of town until M1-09.
replacement: A house price step in the economy (the region's incomes, rates and vacancy), territorial price data, and sellers who are the town's own owners (M1-09).

whatItFakes: American Samoa has no bank branch in the FDIC Summary of Deposits, so its town bank's deposits are the nation's deposits per resident times the town's people. (Guam, the Northern Marianas, Puerto Rico and the Virgin Islands are in the county table with their own FDIC branch deposits, so they no longer use this.)
why: FDIC Summary of Deposits has no rows for American Samoa or the Virgin Islands in the data, and island villages carry no county code.
replacement: American Samoa's bank deposits from its territorial banking regulator or the banks' own reports; checked Oct 19 (claude): the FDIC Summary of Deposits for June 30, 2026 lists 16 branches in Guam, 6 in the Northern Marianas, 260 in Puerto Rico and 20 in the Virgin Islands, all already in data/tables/town-deposits.json, and none in American Samoa.

whatItFakes: Where no ACS tenure or rent table covers a place (American Samoa, Guam, the Northern Marianas, the Virgin Islands), homes are owned in the nation's share and rents and values start at the nation's household-weighted county medians.
why: The American Community Survey does not cover the four island areas; their 2020 Census tables are not in the data yet.
replacement: Census 2020 Island Areas tenure, gross rent and value tables for each island area.

whatItFakes: Where the ACS withholds a county's median rent or home value (a county with very few households: Kalawao, Hawaii; Edwards, Kenedy, Loving and Culberson, Texas), the state's household-weighted county median stands in, then the nation's.
why: Resolved Oct 19 (gov-standins-housing): a county the ACS withholds takes the household-weighted median of its neighboring counties (Census county adjacency, src/core2/data/housing/county-neighbors.json); the state and nation stand in only if no neighbor publishes. world-property-tax-zero-home-values: a missing value read as zero left every owner in the county without a home. world-property-tax-zero-home-values: a missing value read as zero left every owner in the county without a home, so no property tax was collected.
replacement: The county's own median from the ACS 5-year table when it is published, or the median of its neighboring counties.

whatItFakes: A union local's members are the place's employed at its state's 2025 membership rate (the nation's where BLS has no row), paying dues from the wider population's pooled cash; nobody is recorded as a member.
why: The opening records no memberships.
replacement: Members recorded on people (by industry and state, BLS Union Members tables), each choosing to join or leave from their pay, job and views; dues from their own cash.

whatItFakes: The town bank's smallest personal loan is a common published minimum ($1,000), not the bank's own product terms.
why: Community banks' product terms are not in the data.
replacement: A sourced range of community-bank personal loan minimums (FDIC or call-report product data).

whatItFakes: Every owner pays the state's average effective property tax rate, to the outside account, with no assessment cap.
why: The county's rate in force, its cap and its treasury are OPUS-GOV's law in force (lawInForce(api, "property-tax")), on its branch.
replacement: registerPropertyTax with the county's rate, cap and treasury from the law in force.

whatItFakes: Property tax is paid a twelfth each month, as through a mortgage escrow, for every owner.
why: Counties bill once or twice a year on their own dates; the dates come with each county's law.
replacement: Bills on the county's due dates from the law in force, with escrow monthly only for owners with a mortgage.

whatItFakes: A compliance duty costs every bound business twice the manufacturing average pollution-abatement share of its operating costs.
why: No per-industry abatement cost data is loaded yet.
replacement: Census PACE abatement operating costs by industry (NAICS), scaled by the standard the county misses.

whatItFakes: Each household takes a public broadband offer as the subscribing share of one household, not by its own choice.
why: Household subscriptions and switching choices are not modeled per household.
replacement: Each household's subscription and its own choice to switch, from its price and service.

whatItFakes: New houses sell only to full renter households; counted renters and households moving in never buy one, so unsold houses pile up.
why: Counted households' money is pooled by place and arrivals are OPUS-CORE's population engine.
replacement: Counted renter households and arrivals buy new houses through the same choice and mortgage, once fill-in and arrivals land.

whatItFakes: At the opening (before any law can change), Social Security's earliest claim age, full retirement age by birth year and the age-70 end of delayed credits are read from a core data table of the same statute GOV's law rows hold. During play, claims are dated from the law in force (GOV's socialSecurityAges) wherever the laws engine runs; a claim already dated keeps its date if Congress changes the ages later.
why: The retirement claim became a decision within the law's bounds before GOV's laws module carries Social Security ages.
replacement: GOV's Social Security ages as law in force (lawInForce), read at the claim date. Done Oct 15 (claude/ss-ages-law-in-force): retirementClaimAgeMonths takes the ages from the law (socialSecurityAges, the law in force at the claim date, or the day-one law for the opening's history); the core table src/core2/data/social-security-ages.json is deleted.

whatItFakes: People who reach their claim age during play, full or counted, start a Social Security award sized like the opening's (a participant-average amount scaled by modeled covered months), paid monthly by the place's outside payer: to the person, or into their place's residents income while they're counted (it follows them when they're filled in). No application, earnings test, spouse or survivor benefit.
why: WORLD's jobs engine retires people during play, and nothing started their benefits, so retirees lost all income.
replacement: GOV's Social Security program: claims read the law in force and awards follow each person's recorded earnings.

whatItFakes: A town whose opening has no recorded teacher job to copy (no private school) gets no public school district.
why: The district's jobs copy a recorded teacher's job, timetable and pay; the old generator has no public school organization to staff. Resolved Oct 13 (OPUS-CORE): a town with no recorded teacher job gets teachers at the OEWS national median teacher pay on a school-day timetable.
replacement: The opening's jobs builder makes teacher jobs from the occupation's OEWS pay and a school-day timetable without a template.

whatItFakes: A counted worker who retires draws their place's opening retirees' average income (Social Security and pensions from outside the town), not a benefit from their own earnings record and claim age.
why: Counted people have no earnings records; Social Security claims and benefit formulas are OPUS-CORE's and OPUS-GOV's. Resolved Oct 19, 2026: a counted worker who retires claims at once from their own record through claimRetirementNow (modules/retirement-claims.ts), sized as the opening sizes awards; that path stays under SG-CORE-retirement-claims-in-play until the Social Security program.
replacement: The core's Social Security claim for counted retirees, with GOV's benefit rules in force.

whatItFakes: Each outcome the web keeps (crime, schooling, coverage, turnout and the rest) stays at its place's real starting level except where a researched link moves it; nothing else in the world moves it.
why: The research's drift sizes (data/research/outcome-web/place-outcome-bases-2024.json, defaultDrift) include a monthly chance of a society-wide wave, which the no-dice rule forbids; the causes behind drift are not yet modeled.
replacement: Each outcome moved by the engines that cause it (a crime engine, schools, health coverage, elections), with the web's factor on top, and society-wide shifts from recorded causes rather than a monthly chance.

whatItFakes: How strongly each tie holds a person in town and each event pushes them out, and the scale that turns the ACS rate for their age into a monthly pull.
why: The research gives how often people of each age leave a county and the reasons movers give, but not each tie's and event's size in this model.
replacement: Weights checked against ACS departures by age and tenure across drawn places in the M1-09 year run, and against the CPS reasons for moving.

whatItFakes: A person who moved away keeps their town place and household on their record; the inactive tier and the departure record say they left.
why: The core has no call to change a person's place or household mid-run.
replacement: A core call (OPUS-CORE) that moves a person to the destination place and out of their household, so counts, voter rolls and screens read the new place. Done Oct 13 (FIXER-MOVES): the core's relocatePeopleV1 moves leavers to the destination place and county, and out of their household (whole households move with them), so counts, voter rolls and screens read the new place.

whatItFakes: A household that owns its home with a mortgage and has members who stay in town does not leave together; only a grown child in it can move out. A household that leaves entirely sells its home, pays off its mortgage and takes the surplus.
why: Splitting a mortgaged home between those who go and those who stay (who keeps the home and the loan) is not modeled.
replacement: A recorded decision of who keeps a home and its mortgage when some of a household's members leave, so that groups can leave with part of the household behind.

whatItFakes: A person whose job a saved agreement names as its provider's qualification (a visitor's lodging, a public supplier contract) does not move away; moves keeps its own copy of the jobs engine's lookup of those jobs.
why: The core rejects such an agreement's next payment once the job ends, and the jobs engine's lookup is not exported.
replacement: Agreements re-resolve their qualifying worker when a job ends (WORLD/CORE), and the jobs engine exports its pinned-job lookup; then these holders can move like anyone else.
resolvedBy: Same change, October 19, 2026: the moves engine's copy of the lookup is deleted, so a holder of a job a saved agreement names moves like anyone else and the agreement re-resolves at its next payment (finance-cash.ts productJobRelations).

whatItFakes: A person whose recorded income award (a pension, Social Security) is paid into a household other members stay in does not move away yet.
why: An income award and its payment term name the household they are paid into, and the core checks the person is still in it on every payment; moving the person to a new household would break the award's next payment. Resolved Oct 16, 2026 (core-income-award-follows-person): a mover's recipient income contract names the household where they live now and keeps the household the saved award names (moveRecipientIncomeHome); moves no longer holds them.
replacement: A core call (OPUS-CORE) that lets a recorded income award follow its person to a new household when they move, with its own dated record; then these people can move like anyone else.

whatItFakes: While the player skips, the character’s own pick (the core’s chooseAct selection) is resumed as a player answer, so the saved act carries a controlled-choice reason key.
why: The core’s player clock has no resume kind that records an act as the character’s own decision. Resolved by OPUS-PLAY (2026-10-12): the bench resumes with OPUS-CORE's own-choice kind (core2-api-v12), so the act is saved as the character's own decision.
replacement: An OPUS-CORE resume kind that saves the act as the character’s own decision while control is held.

whatItFakes: The bench builds a smaller town (2,000 people by default) instead of the full opening cohort.
why: A day of the full 40,000-person town takes about 13 seconds, too slow to play. Resolved by OPUS-PLAY (2026-10-12): /play builds the whole place two-level (OPUS-CORE), and a year runs in 39 s; the developer page's size field is a tool, not a stand-in.
replacement: OPUS-CORE’s two-level population and speed work, after which the bench builds the full place.

whatItFakes: Every home in the bench shows the shared suburban house interior.
why: New-core households record no dwelling type (apartment, mobile home, rowhouse, farmhouse), so the picture cannot follow the home. Resolved by OPUS-PLAY (2026-10-12): the scene reads OPUS-WORLD's dwellingKind (house, rowhouse, apartment, mobile home, farmhouse) and shows that home's picture.
replacement: A dwelling type on each household from OPUS-WORLD housing or OPUS-PEOPLE, read by the bench scene picker.

whatItFakes: Unemployment insurance is built (a claim after a layoff or closure, the state's law in force, a weekly benefit to the worker) but each benefit is paid from the town's outside account, not from the state's unemployment fund, and nothing collects the employers' contributions into that fund.
why: Narrowed Oct 17 (claude): the row said a spell of unemployment pays nothing; jobs-benefits.ts pays it from the town's outside account. The state fund and the employer contributions into it need the state treasury on the budgets module (M1-07, OPUS-GOV).
replacement: State unemployment insurance under the law in force, paid through postJournal from the state's fund.

whatItFakes: Before a door-knocking round, the bench fills in from the counts as many of the town’s households as the round could reach, so the campaign engine has doors to knock in the two-level world.
why: knockDoors walks only the households already in the core; in the two-level world most of the town is counts.
replacement: OPUS-GOV’s knockDoors (with OPUS-CORE’s fillInPerson) filling in each household it actually reaches.
resolvedBy: Second Session D, October 15, 2026: removed bench fillDoors; campaigns.walkDoors already visits both population tiers and knockDoors fills only the household whose adult actually opens.

whatItFakes: Election night names a drawn challenger by repeating the voting module’s private identity draw (same seed, seat key and role).
why: The voting module draws challengers’ identities privately and exports no name reader.
replacement: An OPUS-GOV export that names any candidate id (resident, official term or drawn challenger). Resolved Oct 16, 2026: election night reads candidateIdentity (src/core2/candidate-identity.ts), exported by the voting module, and the bench's own repeat of the draw is deleted.

whatItFakes: A business whose owner stops working or dies with no worker or family member to take it on keeps running without a recorded owner.
why: The core closes a business only when it can't pay (closeEmployer); there is no voluntary closure for a solvent business yet.
replacement: A core call to wind down a solvent business (end its jobs, contracts and books; the owner keeps what is left), asked of OPUS-CORE; the owner then chooses between closing and selling.
resolvedBy: Second Session D, October 15, 2026: succeed already records no-successor and calls closeByChoice, which uses the core closeBusinessByChoice writer to settle a solvent business. Retired the stale entry after focused closure and played-year checks.

whatItFakes: Where OPUS-WORDS' mined bank has no name for an act yet (care for a relative, join an association, hold a meeting, visit an office), the play screen names its choice button from a bench table of control names (“Look after”).
why: The mined choice-names bank (data/english/parts/choice-names.json) covers about half the core's acts; a raw action id is not something a player should read.
replacement: Mined names for every act in OPUS-WORDS' bank, composed by OPUS-PEOPLE's English engine; then this table is removed.

whatItFakes: A /play town whose opening has a kin move dated after the opening day opens without the core’s opening economy (retirement income, customers) and outside market, on the finance-only route.
why: OPUS-PEOPLE’s opening kin moves can be dated after the opening day, which the core’s retirement-income step refuses (“Past fact outside recipient lifetime/opening”). Resolved Oct 16, 2026 (core-kin-moves-clamped-to-opening): kin moves are dated no later than the opening day (opening-kin.ts), so no town fails the income check; Valmont, Colorado and 15 other drawn places open on the full economy, and the bench's fallback is deleted.
replacement: Opening kin moves dated on or before the opening day (OPUS-PEOPLE), so every town takes the closures route; then this fallback is removed.

whatItFakes: The bench applies the custom-world settings (wages, household cash, outside demand) with its own copy of the core's arithmetic; lean and turnout are recorded on the world but nothing reads them yet.
why: OPUS-CORE's applyOpeningSettings and scaleOutsideSales aren't exported, and no engine reads the politics settings yet (audit 4).
replacement: OPUS-CORE exports its settings step for any opening; OPUS-PEOPLE (views) and OPUS-GOV (turnout, party strength) read placeMetadata.worldSettings.
resolvedBy: Second Session D, October 15, 2026: both openings import core2/world-settings.ts; removed the bench arithmetic copy. Political settings are read by electorate.customPolitics.

whatItFakes: A town department head appointed where no town treasury is open holds the post without pay (with budgets open, they're on the town's payroll); state cabinet members are identities and draw no pay.
why: Public payroll from treasuries is OPUS-CORE's (public employers pay as outside payers today).
replacement: Resolved Oct 19: the state cabinet the governor picks are full people on the state payroll (job:public:state:<post>:<person>), the one replaced leaves it; a town head or an agency head is paid the same way. A world with no treasury open has no payroll, which is not a played world (pool item gov-stopgap-executive-missing-engine).

whatItFakes: Which orders an executive may issue, the state cabinets and the local department heads come from a research file written from memory (data/research/executive/executive-powers-2026.json, every row an estimate); only the voting-rights order (documented in Virginia, Kentucky and Iowa) is offered.
why: The research helper fetched no sources; verification against state constitutions, Book of the States Table 4.10 and NCSL is still to do.
replacement: Each row verified against its cited source, and more orders offered as their engines exist.

whatItFakes: Every owner's property tax goes to the county treasury (the city's, else the state's, where there's no county government), which keeps every level's share.
why: The county's rate in force is every level's tax together (Census ACS median taxes over median value); remitting the city's and the school district's shares needs payees with shares in WORLD's billing, or a remittance step. Resolved by OPUS-GOV (2026-10-13): owners pay the county's tax collector, which remits each levying government's share monthly by its per-resident Census property-tax revenue (budgets.ts remitPropertyTax).
replacement: The collector remits each level's share by its Census property-tax revenue line, on the county's own due dates.

whatItFakes: 60 of 261 statewide executive offices (superintendents, insurance, labor and land commissioners, commissions and boards, D.C. and the territories) take their holder's party from rows not verified against a live source (data/research/offices/statewide-executive-parties-2026.json); 201 rows were verified against Wikipedia's current officeholder lists on 2026-10-13.
why: Ballotpedia and NASS couldn't be fetched, and Wikipedia has no current list for those offices.
replacement: Every row checked against Ballotpedia's partisan composition pages or the state's own records.

whatItFakes: Each month, a state, county, city or federal treasury receives from the town's outside account an even twelfth of the yearly revenue no flow in the game pays (state and federal aid come from the treasury above it; corporate, customs, excise, estate and gift, selective sales and vehicle taxes come from named groups of payers on their due dates), and pays each spending line an even twelfth: what the town's engines paid on the line stays in town, the town's share of purchases goes to its businesses, and the rest goes to the outside account as spending elsewhere.
why: Real payers outside the town (the rest of the state's taxpayers, fee payers) and real payees (contractors and public workers elsewhere) aren't modeled; their real dates (aid schedules, tax due dates, payrolls) aren't in data yet.
replacement: Each revenue line from its real payer on its real dates, and each spending line to its real payees on theirs.

whatItFakes: A government's charges and fees (tuition, hospital bills, sewer and trash, parks, tolls) are paid by the town's households in proportion to the living cost each pays on the 1st, split by what the charges are for from the Census 2022 item codes; no household chooses to use a service, no business pays a charge of its own, and a household that uses none still pays its share of the living cost.
why: gov-outside-revenue-fees-wiring (p1): the fees line was an even twelfth from the outside account that no household or business paid. The game does not yet model each service's use (a student's tuition, a hospital stay, a sewer bill by dwelling), so the charges follow what a household spends.
replacement: Each service paid by the people who use it on the day they use it: tuition by enrolled students' households, hospital charges by patients' visits, sewer and trash by dwellings and businesses, parks and tolls by trips, from the school, health and travel engines.

whatItFakes: When a couple has no dated partner fact (or it is dated the opening day), the partnership start is estimated: one birth-spacing interval before their first child, else the mother reaching the usual age of a first union.
why: The opening writes partnerships without a start date for many couples, so a long marriage looked brand new on the opening day.
replacement: Partnerships carry their own recorded start date from the opening's partnership model (OPUS-PEOPLE, opening-partnership).

whatItFakes: Households that move into the counted population are generated in the shape of a household already recorded in the place (ages, sexes, who is family), with new names and temperaments from the world's seed, and arrive with no job, contracts, cash or past on record. Counted babies and newcomers' children get temperaments without their parents' inheritance links.
why: The counts need arrivals at the ACS rate now; the jobs, purchase and housing engines do not yet take newcomers into their books. Resolved Oct 17 (claude): the births engine's own arrival path is deleted; households move in through the counted-moves engine (src/core2/modules/counted-moves.ts), which is installed with every counted world, and the newborns' temperament part is registered as SG-PW8-counted-newborn-temperament.
replacement: Newcomers are generated by the population builder for the place (OPUS-CORE), join the job seekers (OPUS-WORLD jobs) and take a home and purchase contracts (housing, residents flows).

whatItFakes: A counted baby gets a temperament drawn from the world's seed for its age and place, without its parents' temperaments passed on.
why: Counted parents carry no inheritance links in the counts, so the family model that passes traits to a full person's child has nothing to read.
replacement: A counted baby inherits from its counted parents' packed traits through the same family model a full person's child uses.

whatItFakes: A counted resident's engagement with politics, computed with a copy of the views engine's formula (their own key spread around the CES cell average) so the candidacy screen matches the value they get when filled in.
why: The views engine (src/core2/modules/views.ts, OPUS-PEOPLE) keeps the formula private to viewOf; the counted screen needs the same value without filling everyone in. Resolved Oct 16: views.ts exports countedEngagement (and viewOf uses the same helper), candidacy calls it, and the copy is deleted.
replacement: OPUS-PEOPLE exports an engagement function from views.ts that takes a counted record; candidacy calls it and this copy is removed.

whatItFakes: The villages of Guam, the U.S. Virgin Islands, American Samoa and the Northern Mariana Islands come from the game's existing recorded list (carried over from the old place module), not from Census identities.
why: The Census Gazetteer corpus covers the states, D.C. and Puerto Rico only; the island areas need their own identities.
replacement: Census 2020 Island Areas place identities (the research request territory-place-identities), read into the same listing. Oct 14 (OPUS-CORE): the candidate list is built (src/core2/data/places/territory-places-census.json, 158 inhabited villages with Census GEOIDs and 2020 populations, every current key kept, by tooling/build-territory-places.ts); the swap waits until PEOPLE's population builder reads places through the core lookup.

whatItFakes: The town's families with school-age children are ranked by cash per child and the best-off enroll all their children in the private school until the town's private share of school-age children (NCES) is reached, each paying the average private tuition. The family's beliefs, the schools nearby and the child's own needs do not yet enter, and enrollment is fixed at the opening.
why: Private schools had no customers at all, so they closed in every town.
replacement: PEOPLE's schools engine: each child's enrollment chosen from the family's income, beliefs and the schools nearby, moving as they change. Means-ranked enrollment replaced the even spread of the town's average on Oct 19.

whatItFakes: The wider population's deaths and births come from rates applied to the counts each month: SSA cohort life tables scaled by the state's 2017 age-adjusted death rate against the nation's (NCHS), and NCHS 2024 national birth rates by mother's age. Whoever has the highest rate is the one who dies or gives birth; nobody's health or family plans decide it.
why: The counted population never changed (owner, Oct 12: the counted rest drifts too).
replacement: Deleted Oct 17 (claude/counted-drift-delete): the counted births and deaths are the renewal engine's counted flows (src/core2/births-counted.ts: NCHS state birth rates by mother's age, life-table chances with the state's death-rate ratio, deaths following serious illnesses), registered under SG-PW8-counted-arrivals; the old drift module ran only in life cores without the renewal engine and stood down in every played world.

whatItFakes: Newcomers to the wider population arrive only into homes a counted household just left, as a household of the same ages and genders with the home's cash, given names people born their year were called (SSA) and a family name drawn from the town's recorded names, and no retirement income or job (the jobs engine may hire them). The town's own state rates apply to every counted household, including relatives' households elsewhere. Leavers' cash stays in town.
why: The counted population should move in and out (owner, Oct 12, ruling 4), and no housing market places counted newcomers yet.
replacement: Deleted Oct 17 (claude/counted-drift-delete): counted people move between places from causes in the counted-moves engine (src/core2/modules/counted-moves.ts), and newcomers are generated by the renewal engine's counted flows (SG-PW8-counted-arrivals); the drift module's own newcomer rule is gone.

whatItFakes: A counted worker whose job a public supplier agreement names as its qualified worker never dies or moves away in the counts.
why: A public supplier agreement's qualification must resolve its named job each month, and nothing yet lets an agreement replace a worker who left.
replacement: When a named worker leaves, the agreement names another qualified worker at the supplier or ends (the finance engine's public supplier rules). Done Oct 14 (OPUS-CORE): supplier agreements now follow whoever does the work and end when nobody does (5ea270be on main), so named counted workers die and move like anyone else.

whatItFakes: Every school-age full person attends the town's public school district (or, in a world opened without it, their town's schools as a place) on the weekdays of one national school calendar (Sept. 1 to June 10, cut at the state's required instructional days where it sets them in days (Education Commission of the States, 2018), the federal holidays by their dates each year, and fixed winter and spring breaks), for the national average school day. Attending is their own choice through the chooser against a full compulsory pull, so in practice every child goes every day: no illness, truancy or family circumstance keeps one home. No grade, class, teacher, homework, private school or homeschooling.
why: School-age people never went to school (M0-13).
replacement: PEOPLE's schools engine: each child's enrolled school (opening-schools), its district calendar and hours, classes with classmates and teachers, and attendance that state law and family circumstances shape.

whatItFakes: Disasters happen only where and when FEMA declared one for the town's county or state (since 2000), as a public news event on the incident's start date. Federal Public Assistance obligated to the county's own government and the town's government (disasters declared since 2020) is paid in full on the declaration date from the U.S. Treasury outside account the game already keeps for Social Security. FEMA housing assistance approved for the town's households (Individuals and Households Program, owners and renters, disasters since 2020) is paid to the town's counted residents on the declaration date, scaled by the world's people over the Census estimate (a town without an estimate takes the whole amount); no single household is chosen, and 36% of household rows don't match a county or town by name. A government kept outside the world receives nothing. The town's households also pay, on the declaration date, for repairing the damage FEMA inspected in owners' homes (scaled the same way), to the town's open builders by their staff or to builders outside the town; the news event carries how many homes FEMA found damaged. Damage to rented homes falls on no landlord, and repairs are paid at once from what households have rather than over months or by insurance. No damage to businesses, public buildings or people; no other applicants (schools, utilities, nonprofits; 13% of assistance rows don't match a county); no new disasters after the records end.
why: The core owns disasters and hazards (BOARD); under no-dice a rate can't decide when one strikes, and the owner hasn't ruled on what should cause new ones.
replacement: The owner's ruling on what causes a disaster in play; damage to businesses, public buildings and people (from NOAA storm episodes), and household aid and repairs reaching the named households that lost homes, with insurance and repairs over time; assistance paid over its real obligation dates to every applicant; a federal FEMA account of its own.

whatItFakes: The national mood that moves every voter's choice for the president's party is read from the national economy since the opening (unemployment and inflation) and the midterm penalty, with no presidential approval behind it.
why: No engine records the president's approval yet (the executive's record and the public's view of it).
replacement: Presidential approval read from the president's own record and the public's views (the executive engine and the views engine), moving the president's party's candidates by its measured effect on the vote.

whatItFakes: A township board's ordinances are written as the town's own local law (the place level of the law chain), and a township board only legislates where no town council does; the law chain has no township level, so a township's ordinances and a village council's inside it can't both stand.
why: Towns governed by a township board never legislated at all: only councils and county boards met (Oct 13 lawmaking-volume fix).
replacement: A township level in the law chain (laws-starting.ts) with its own starting law and enactments, so a township board and a village council inside it each legislate for their own jurisdiction.
resolution: The law chain has a township level between the county and the city (laws-starting.ts), and a township board legislates for its own township jurisdiction (the government-unit id) alongside a council in the same place; sales-tax shares and withholding read the level.

whatItFakes: A holder whose party the roster doesn't record (a statewide executive such as an attorney general or treasurer, or a legislative seat with no roster row) sits in the party that carried the state in 2024; a lieutenant governor on the governor's ticket takes the governor's party.
why: The offices research records each statewide office's term and vacancy rule but not its holder's party, and the legislative roster has no row for a few seats.
replacement: Each statewide executive's real party from a public roster (Ballotpedia's partisan composition of state executive offices, or each state's own election results).

whatItFakes: A sitting president or governor at home is shown outside the White House or the governor's residence by day and in the large house's living room at night, because neither residence has painted rooms.
why: The Firefly library has the residences' exteriors only; the bench lists the rooms' picture names first (officialResidences in src/bench/data/scene-places.json) so they are used as soon as they are painted.
replacement: Painted rooms for each residence (white-house-residence-living, -dining, -bedroom; governor-residence-living, -dining, -bedroom), imported under those names.

whatItFakes: Each approved look is painted doing one thing, so a person whose look doesn't fit where they are (a teen boy's skateboard or basketball indoors, a laptop off work) is drawn in their next look, or the nearest-age look that fits: indoors, a teen boy is drawn with the youngest adult look in a hoodie. The player's teen and adult looks are tied by two hand-paired families (family-066, family-009) chosen by skin, hair and clothes.
why: The approved art has 4 teen and 4 child looks, one activity each, and no adult version of any teen look.
replacement: The CTO's art in docs/coordination/people-art-requests.md: activity variants of every look, 12 teen and 12 child looks per sex, and the adult version of each teen look with a shared family id.

whatItFakes: The opening's public employers in town (schools, police, fire, county offices) pay their workers from outside accounts; the treasury's lines for that work pay the outside account instead of those employers.
why: Linking the opening's public employers to a treasury is a core change (public owner records, work-cash.ts; SG-P8-public-payroll-due-flow).
replacement: Each public employer draws its payroll from its government's treasury, and the close counts it as that line's in-town spending.
resolvedBy: Claude Sonnet session, October 16, 2026: the budgets engine calls api.fundPublicPay for every opening public employer, linking it to its government's treasury (matched by government key); the employer's wages leave the treasury's account on the payday journal, the close counts them as that line's in-town spending, and what the treasury couldn't cover is a public-pay shortfall on the month's treasury row. What the lines still pay the outside account is spending outside the town's employers.

whatItFakes: When the federal Social Security line is cut or raised, the retirement awards the opening wrote for full people keep their amount; only awards claimed during play follow the line.
why: The finance engine refuses to change the amount of a recipient-income contract (setStandingContractAmount in finance-state.ts, OPUS-CORE). Resolved Oct 16, 2026 (core-opening-award-level-rerate): a recipient income contract takes a new amount from its next due date (setRecipientIncomeAmount), the measure and day are recorded beside the saved award, and the outside funding that pays its payer moves by the same dollars; applySocialSecurityLevel sets them.
replacement: setStandingContractAmount accepts a recipient-income contract's new benefit level from its next due date, and applySocialSecurityLevel sets it, with the funding contract that pays it.

whatItFakes: A cause group spends its money only on ad time, bought through the campaigns engine's ad purchase; it holds no events, sends no mailers and pays none of a cause's own costs.
why: Stress audit defect 2 (Oct 14): groups took donations and never spent them. The ad purchase was the one existing way to buy reach.
replacement: A group chooses among the reach it can buy (events, mailers, press) and a cause's costs (a lawyer, a petition drive where the golden path needs one), read from its members' plans.

whatItFakes: No appointer ever names the player to a town post; the player holds a post only by appointing others as the executive or by winning a seat.
why: Trace audit (Oct 14), item 3: in Tillamook, Oregon (seed 19a393194ce9) the player was appointed public works director with no choice of theirs. The player's decisions are always theirs. Whether an appointer may offer the player a post, for the player to accept or decline, is the owner's call.
replacement: The owner's ruling: either the player is never appointed, or an appointer's choice of the player becomes an offer the player accepts or declines in the conversation, and only an accepted offer fills the post.
resolution: docs/coordination/OWNER-DECISIONS.md, 'The player's choices are the player's' (Oct 14, night): 'No engine accepts a job, a home, a filing or any choice for the controlled person; the engine offers, the player decides.' Appointers never fill a post with the player on their own; an offer is the player's to accept.

whatItFakes: An estate pays no estate or inheritance tax: no tax series exists for it in the law catalog yet.

whatItFakes: A territory's prior governor race (Puerto Rico and American Samoa only; Guam, the Northern Marianas and the Virgin Islands read their reported governor ballots, and every territory with a delegate total reads it for the delegate race) counts only the town's own ballots, since territories cast no presidential vote to scale from.

whatItFakes: A counted employer short of cash on payday records a wage shortfall and never draws its approved credit line, though the line has room.

whatItFakes: A relative living out of town (a husk) is never an aide candidate, because the records hold no work for them, and an unknown job is not an empty one.

whatItFakes: Payroll withholding for a worker who lives outside the town reads the law of the worker's residence from the starting-law rows (the town's recorded rows where a jurisdiction is shared with the town), so a law enacted in play in a jurisdiction the town does not share is not read; a residence the place lookup cannot resolve gets federal and payroll tax only.

whatItFakes: Income tax a worker owes a government with no treasury in the world (another state, or a county or city the world does not model) is not withheld, so the worker's pay is not reduced by it and no money moves.
why: An outside account takes money only against a resolved due-obligation record, and those governments have no treasury account to pay. Resolved Oct 16 (world-withholding-outside-governments): each such government is an outside government with an account, and the tax is withheld and paid to it against a due record the withholding writes.

whatItFakes: A local flat income tax on a row whose base is wages or AGI is taken on the paycheck's gross pay (no pre-tax contributions or personal exemptions are modeled); a row whose base is taxable income is taken after the state (else federal) standard deduction only.
why: The law rows name the base but carry no exemption or adjustment amounts, and workers' pre-tax deductions are not modeled.
replacement: Personal exemptions and adjustments read from the law rows and the worker's own records.

whatItFakes: A worker who lives outside the town pays no county or city income tax to the town's jurisdictions for working there (the rows' nonresident rate is not applied); local tax is withheld only by the law at the worker's residence.

replacement: Resolve the workplace's local chain per paycheck and apply each row's nonresident rate to residents of other jurisdictions.

whatItFakes: Employers pay no Social Security or Medicare share on wages paid to counted workers through the residents' merged wage flows; only full workers' paychecks carry the employer share.

Built Oct 16: the residents engine tells every module each counted payday (onCountedWages) and the employer-taxes module posts the share, per worker times the workers the flow pays.

whatItFakes: An official whose office sits outside the town (a state or federal office, at its seat of government) draws one applicant living where the office sits, generated from the world's seed and the office (name, age in the business-worker range, traits), and records them as a person only when hired.
why: The owner ruled that such an official hires from where the office sits (Oct 14), but the seat's population isn't modeled, so there is no labor market there to read.
replacement: The seat's coarse population (people by age and work, as the town's counted population is kept), from which the official's applicants come by the same reach and working-age reads.

whatItFakes: How soon a body may undo a law it passed: no place's data records a reconsideration rule, so a sliding reluctance (fresher law and wider margin, more reluctance; a member's own last vote) stands in for the rule.

replacement: The owner's ruling on reconsideration, and each place's recorded rule as data where one exists.

whatItFakes: A person without a seat asking a member they know to carry a bill, and the member's answer from their own position on it, their tie to the asker and the asker's standing; built ahead of the owner's confirmation.

replacement: The owner's confirmation of the carry request (or its replacement); then this row resolves.
resolution: Owner ruling (docs/coordination/OWNER-DECISIONS.md, player-path audit, confirmed by the owner): a loser can 'ask a council member they know to carry a bill (the constituent path)'. The member decides by their own position and the asker's standing (OPUS-GOV, Oct 14).

whatItFakes: One national rule for how a mayor or county executive brings a bill of their own: through a member who carries it at their request. Charters differ (some let the mayor introduce ordinances directly).

whatItFakes: How much traits, ties, evidence, prominence, party, money and the prosecutor's record weigh at each step from a report to a sentence.

whatItFakes: A state prosecutor's office where the offices data has neither a county prosecutor covering the town nor an elected attorney general.
why: Appointed attorneys general and territorial prosecutors are not in the offices data.
replacement: Appointed attorneys general and territorial attorneys general as offices in the offices data, with their appointing rule.

whatItFakes: Bribery is sentenced on the place's lowest felony-assault range from the sentencing research, not on the place's own bribery statute.

replacement: Each place's bribery-of-a-public-official grade and range read into data/research/justice/sentencing-ranges-2026.json, read by offense key.

whatItFakes: Every place vacates an office on a felony conviction, on the day of the conviction, and forfeits all of a bribe's proceeds.
why: The common rule in state constitutions and codes; each state's rule and its timing (conviction, sentencing or final appeal) are not read.
replacement: Each state's forfeiture-of-office rule and timing, and its rule for forfeiting a bribe's proceeds, as data by state.

whatItFakes: The justice engine writes a prisoner's discretionary-choice flag on the person directly, because the core's updatePerson does not take it.

whatItFakes: The player's report and plea are decided by the character's own traits and the case's reads, like anyone else's, instead of being offered to the player.

replacement: The plea and the report offered to the player as choices in the hearing scene, through the director.

whatItFakes: A job the jobs engine gives a person in prison is ended by the justice engine before its first shift, instead of the jobs engine never hiring them.

Staff candidates and the shared public payroll writer also read custody. Justice ends only jobs held when imprisonment begins; the daily repair is removed.

whatItFakes: A convicted official keeps the bribe they took; the court collects only the fine.
why: The small justice engine sentences and fines; forfeiture of the proceeds (18 U.S.C. 981 and the states' forfeiture laws) is not built.

whatItFakes: An outlet's revenue (its audience's subscriptions and the advertising they see) is one standing monthly payment from the town's outside customers, sized at the opening from its audience and an estimated amount per follower per year by kind; local businesses do not buy ads, households' own reading spending still goes to the outside account, and the payment does not follow the audience as it grows or shrinks. whatItFakes: An interview's answers carry the conversation's moves (plain, further, turn, brief) and the lie as record data, but the screen does not yet open the interview through the director's conversation, so the player cannot see the reporter's questions as spoken lines or pick a move from worded choices.

whatItFakes: Readers of a printed story learn which outlet printed what (the perceived fact printed:<outlet>:story), which bring-it-up's matcher reads, but bring-it-up's data has no change row for a printed story yet, so no one says it aloud.

Resolved Oct 16 (gov-stopgap-press-desk-missing-record): bring-it-up-rows.json has a news.read change row for a printed story, with bank lines naming the outlet and the topic, and a reader who read it says it aloud.

whatItFakes: A press person who lives outside the town (a station group's owner, a station news director, a national outlet's staff) is seated alone in their own household with no rent, living costs or family, as the core's identity fill-in makes them. whatItFakes: A reporter's closeness to a candidate gives access (asked first, the friendly reporter asks) and gentler copy, but a candidate cannot do a reporter a favor, and a reporter cannot hold a story back for a friend. whatItFakes: People of an outlet who live outside the town (every owner of a station or national outlet, a station's news director, the national tier's staff) hold no job and draw no pay, and a national outlet has no revenue or books.

Resolved Oct 16 (claude/gov-stopgap-press-faked-mechanic): a reporter or editor leaves with the job they hold and the jobs engine's hire into the opening is filled in as the outlet's new staff, followed to the desk in src/core2/press-turnover.test.ts.

whatItFakes: A full person's estate is only their cash and the standing payments they owed: homes, loans, businesses and accounts other than their main one are not settled.

whatItFakes: The federal government and other states pay their officials, and receive heirless estates, as outside governments, since only the town's own governments keep treasuries and the town's federal treasury holds only the town's own taxes. Resolved Oct 16 (gov-official-salary-through-payroll): each monthly salary is a gross paycheck from the town's state treasury with the law's withholding taken out to each government that keeps a treasury, the pay is counted as spending on the treasury's administration line, and each figure carries its provenance (governors SOURCED for 2023; the rest ESTIMATED with a spread). replacement: A salaried pay basis in the payroll engine so officials are paid by paycheck with withholding; every state's treasury where its officials act; sourced salary rows for every elected office.

whatItFakes: Only the employers' group, formed against a wage bill, has a lobbyist who weighs a bribe; a bill that costs people money any other way draws no bribe, because its losses aren't measured per payer.

whatItFakes: An official who helps a resident looking for work refers them to the workforce office, but the jobs engine doesn't read the referral when employers pick applicants, so the help changes nothing yet.

whatItFakes: For a bound policy other than an energy-pricing law or a data privacy law (priced by the price engine and the business engine's cost review), what it costs each employer it binds is an estimated share of the employer's payroll (boundEmployerCostShare), except laws that price energy (clean electricity standard, carbon price), which cost each employer its own energy costs by the price engine's arithmetic. replacement: Each law-reach policy that binds employers moves its own money (a price, a fee, a compliance cost), and the stake reads that.

whatItFakes: One national bar on when a local recall may start (not in a term's first 180 days; not again in a term after one failed), not each state's own statute.
why: The owner's ruling (Oct 14): the recall rule reads the place's statute (grounds, signatures, cooling period). The municipal rule pack holds grounds, threshold and circulation window, but no cooling period yet.
replacement: Each state's recall timing bars read into the municipal rule pack and resolved like its threshold and window.

whatItFakes: A business a counted resident owns pays no tax on its profit: under the law its profit is its owner's income, and only owners who are full people pay it (as estimated payments from their own cash). Businesses owned by another organization pay the corporate rate each quarter.

replacement: The counted owner group's share of the profit taxed by the income tax law in force where they live, as a flow of the owner group.

Proved in src/core2/profit-pass-through.test.ts.

whatItFakes: Businesses pay no property tax on their premises; the property-tax engine bills homes only.
why: A business's books record no premises or their value, so there is nothing for the property-tax rate in force to read.

whatItFakes: The record a screen would read for a business's books (cash, sales, costs, wages, profit, taxes paid and owed, its credit line) is built, but no screen shows it: whether a player sees another business's books is the owner's open decision.

replacement: The owner's ruling on who sees a business's books (its owner, the player as owner, public filings only, or anyone), after which OPUS-PLAY shows this record on the screen that ruling names.

whatItFakes: Until the town has at least macroTownGrowthMinMonths of recorded income with the same months a year earlier (about 15 months into a game), the national step hears a neutral stand-in for the town's income growth: trend growth plus the inflation anchor.

replacement: The town's income history before the start (from the opening's pre-start years), so growth is read from the first month.

Actual observed growth still enters the same model; missing pre-start income history remains explicitly registered as SG-WORLD-macro-income-history.

whatItFakes: Engines that still read counted people one by one (jobs, business, campaigns, retirement claims, housing, place prices, candidacy) get a person or household record built on demand from the counted group's packed columns, with no past, no ties outside the household and no sources of their own.

whatItFakes: A town's districts are the state House districts its population splits into (from the place-district join), else the whole town; city council wards are not modeled.

whatItFakes: A counted person built at fill-in has their household, job and coworkers but no relatives living outside their household.
why: Counted people keep no ties outside their household (one model, two tiers); building relatives at fill-in needs the relative generator to run for one person. The owner has not ruled whether that is needed for early access.
replacement: The owner's ruling; if wanted, the opening's relative generator run for one filled-in household, seeded by the world.

The world-has-a-past work merged Oct 11 to 14.

whatItFakes: A full person out of the player's life for 180 days returns to their counted group (TUNABLE).
why: The owner asked for demotion after 'a long while' without naming how long.
