resolution: Owner ruling, Oct 15, 2026: 'The days without contact before a met person drifts back into the counted population is a per-world range of 180 to 240 days, drawn once per world at generation (seeded generation is allowed), never a single fixed number.' Built in counted-demotion.ts (demotionDays) from the countedDemotionDays spread.

whatItFakes: Money an engine pays to or takes from a place's counted residents as a whole (an owner's draw to owners who are counted, a pooled property tax bill, a price change on counted households, money left in the place's residents account) is shared by the place's counted groups by their people, not by the households it belongs to.
why: Those engines (business, housing property tax, place prices, unemployment claims) name a place or a counted person but pay the place's residents account; until each passes the person or household, the groups share it.
replacement: Each engine pays counted money through countedPayment with the counted person or household it belongs to (business owners, property tax by owner household, price changes by household), so the right group pays or is paid.

whatItFakes: A town split between state legislative districts places its counted households into the districts by income order, filling each district in proportion to its Census population in the town, so each district holds a slice of the town's income ladder.
why: The game reads only each district's population in the town (Census place-district populations); it has no district-level income, housing or vote tables, and no home locations.
replacement: Each district's own Census tables (ACS by state legislative district: income, tenure, age) and its election results, so households are placed by the district's real mix.

whatItFakes: A filled-in household keeps its share of the place's unplaced workers' pay (counted workers no employer's books hold) as its own flow, untaxed, until it returns to the counts.
why: The opening places only some counted workers in recorded jobs; the rest are paid from one place-level flow with no employer to file a W-2.
replacement: The jobs engine places every counted worker in a recorded job on an employer's books, so a filled-in worker always gets a real job and withholding.

whatItFakes: A town larger than the opening target (10,000 people, owner decision Oct 9) opens with 10,000 people, not its Census population, so its counts, a law's reach and its money cover only those 10,000. A town smaller than the target opens at its real Census size.
why: The owner set the 10,000 target on Oct 9 before the counted tier was one record per group; whether a bigger town should count its full Census population (each counted household standing for several) is his call.
replacement: The owner's ruling: either keep the cap, or let each counted group of a bigger town carry its Census count with the money and reach scaled to it.
resolution: docs/coordination/OWNER-DECISIONS.md, 'Town size (day-one audit)': 'a town opens at its real Census size; nothing pads it to 10,000. Follows one model, two tiers (counts must match the place).' Open for the engineers: population.ts still caps a town above the target; it follows the ruling next.

whatItFakes: Every town's and county's body numbers its ordinances the same way, by the year and order of introduction ("2026-12"), and opens them with the same 'Be it ordained by' clause, not each place's own style.
why: The owner's ruling (Oct 14): bills follow the real form of their body. States and Congress have recorded numbering and enacting clauses; local bodies' styles are not in the data yet.
replacement: Each place's ordinance numbering and enacting clause read from its code of ordinances into the municipal rule pack, the way its recall rules are.

whatItFakes: A council or board meets on its own rule for the bills placed before it, but the meetings where members file their own ordinances keep the world-legislating engine's tunable yearly count, so one body has two sets of meeting dates.
why: The world-legislating engine is OPUS-GOV's and is being rewritten on its sessions branch; office-day may not edit it.
replacement: world-legislating's scheduleMeeting reads nextMeeting from office-day-calendar.ts, so every meeting of a body is one meeting on one rule. Done Oct 15 (claude/office-local-39): scheduleMeeting in world-legislating.ts reads nextMeeting from office-day-calendar.ts; the tunable localRegularMeetingsPerYear is deleted.

whatItFakes: Ordinances other members file at a regular meeting are voted at the start of the meeting's day, before the player's stop at the meeting's hour, so the player's character votes them on its own even when the player is at the meeting.
why: The world-legislating engine files and votes in one calendar step at midnight; holding the vote until the player's scene needs a change in OPUS-GOV's engine. Resolved Oct 20, 2026: world-legislating files a local meeting's ordinances the day before when the player sits on the body and holds the clock (registerMeetingHold), office-day puts them on the meeting's agenda, and the player takes them up or the meeting closes (office-day-member-filings.test.ts).
replacement: world-legislating splits a local meeting into filing (the agenda) and the vote, with a hook that lets office-day hold the vote until the player's meeting scene takes it up.

whatItFakes: When the player leaves the desk to the character, office-day recomputes the sign-or-veto lean (position plus temperament scaled by how settled the law is) from the legislature engine's exported parts, a copy of the rule other executives use.
why: The legislature engine keeps its executive's own decision inside executiveAction and does not export it. Resolved Oct 16 (OPUS-PLAY session): the legislature exports executiveLean, the one lean every executive follows, and office-day's own-choice signing calls it; the copy is deleted.
replacement: The legislature engine exports the executive's own sign-or-veto choice and office-day calls it.

whatItFakes: A part-time local seat's stipend is a monthly transfer from the town's or county's treasury, counted on its books, not a paycheck, so no income tax or payroll tax is withheld from it.
why: The core allows one job per person, and most council members and commissioners keep a day job; a second, salaried pay basis in the payroll engine does not exist yet (the same gap as SG-CORE-official-salary).
replacement: A salaried second pay basis in the payroll engine (OPUS-CORE), so a stipend is a paycheck with withholding alongside the holder's own job. Built Oct 16: the stipend goes through withholdPay as an official's salary does, on the year's pay with the holder's own job.

whatItFakes: When the player's office hours come and the player has not decided a case, office-day decides it by the character's sense of duty (the base share of officials who help, tilted by traits), a copy of the rule the constituent-cases engine uses for a case nobody decided.
why: The constituent-cases engine keeps that rule inside its own response-window handler and does not export it. Resolved Oct 16: the cases engine exports ownCaseDecision, the one rule for a case nobody decided; office hours in the office day and in the state day call it, and the copies are deleted.
replacement: The constituent-cases engine exports the office's own decision on a case, and office-day calls it.

whatItFakes: Election day always stops the player at the polls; the player cannot set it to run in the background.
why: Two rulings meet here: the engine never casts the player's ballot (owner, October 13, 2026), and what the player does not stop for still happens, done by the character (owner, October 14, 2026).
replacement: The owner's ruling: either the character may cast the player's ballot from its own views when election day is not a stop, or election day stays a stop that cannot be turned off.
resolution: docs/coordination/OWNER-DECISIONS.md (Oct 13): 'The player casts their own ballot ... the engine never votes for the player'; 'Election day is a scene. The player goes to their polling place and marks a ballot there; the vote is cast in the scene, never in a menu.' Election day stays a stop.

whatItFakes: The federal officeholder's day keeps its own small tables (the player's stop settings, the week they chose, the day and act records) and finishes the day itself, because OFFICE-LOCAL's one office-day engine is not built yet.
why: The package puts one engine under every level; FEDERAL may not write it and was told to build against the smallest stand-in until it lands. Resolved by OFFICE-FEDERAL (2026-10-14): the federal day runs on OFFICE-LOCAL's engine (src/core2/modules/office-day.ts); its stops, act record, holds and the player's own vote are the engine's, and the stand-in tables are deleted.
replacement: OFFICE-LOCAL's src/core2/modules/office-day.ts: the federal rows (stops, week, acts) register with it and this module's tables are deleted.

whatItFakes: Dev mode's custom start as a sitting federal officeholder: the player continues as an eligible adult and takes the seat by writing the offices engine's term and the officials engine's record directly; the record's loyalty and ambition copy the predecessor's.
why: Dev mode has no seating of its own and the officials engine builds a record only for drawn officials and its own candidates, not for a person the player controls. Resolved by OFFICE-FEDERAL (2026-10-14): the player takes the sitting member or president with the bench's own BenchPlayer.select; the custom start that seated a town adult is deleted.
replacement: A dev-mode custom start owned by OFFICE-LOCAL or OPUS-PLAY that seats any person through the offices and officials engines, with a record built from the person's own traits.

whatItFakes: A member learns what the floor takes up today by reading the legislature's calendar keys for scheduled votes; a bill the floor brings up the same day it is filed cannot stop the player and is voted by the character through the legislature's beforeVote hook.
why: The legislature keeps no floor agenda a member can read ahead of the vote. Resolved Oct 16: the legislature exports floorAgendaOn and the federal day reads it; a bill the floor takes up the day it is filed has no morning to stop the player and is voted by the character through the legislature hook, which is how the floor works, not a fake.
replacement: OPUS-GOV exports the chamber's floor agenda by date (the floor weeks on gov/sessions), read here in place of the calendar keys.

whatItFakes: A member of Congress's district office takes cases through the cases engine, but the engine brings residents' problems only to the town's own council members and mayor, so a member of Congress receives none.
why: The cases engine (OPUS-GOV) lists only local officials as people a resident may bring a problem to. Resolved by OFFICE-FEDERAL (2026-10-14): removed with the stand-in; casework for members of Congress waits on OPUS-GOV's cases engine routing residents' problems to them, asked on the PR, with no code standing in.
replacement: OPUS-GOV routes a resident's problem to the town's members of Congress as well (a federal problem, such as a wage complaint under the federal floor, to the federal office), and the federal day reads those cases unchanged.
resolution: The cases engine routes a wage complaint under the federal floor to the town's House member and senators (constituent-cases.ts, bringCases); other problems still go to the officials nearest home. Proved in src/core2/federal-casework.test.ts.

whatItFakes: The people a traveler meets in a town other than the player's are recorded identities of that place (drawn from the world's seed and the town), with no household, job or other records there beyond the meeting.
why: Only the player's town has a counted population; other places are kept coarser.
replacement: The other places' coarser populations (OPUS-CORE's wider world) fill in a met person from that place's own counts, as the player's town does.

whatItFakes: The president has no executive order an engine carries: the list is empty.
why: The executive engine's orders read only a state's powers (one orderable series, a governor's).
replacement: OPUS-GOV adds the president's orderable powers (federal series an engine reads, cited) to the executive engine; the federal day lists them and issues through issueOrder.

whatItFakes: The president has no conviction to pardon: the list is empty.
why: The justice engine tries every crime under the state's law and records no federal prosecution.
replacement: OPUS-GOV's justice engine records the prosecuting sovereign and exports a pardon that ends a federal sentence; the federal day lists federal convictions.

whatItFakes: The situation room never opens: no crisis is listed.
why: Main keeps no record of a disaster, attack or other national crisis (the real disasters are on OPUS-CORE's unmerged branch).
replacement: The federal day opens the situation room on the crisis records (disasters first), with the cabinet secretary whose department answers it.
resolution: The federal day opens the situation room on the disasters engine's hazard.disaster records (crisesToday in src/core2/office-day-federal-president.ts): each incident stays listed for the situationRoomOpenDays after it begins, with the cabinet department that answers its type (Homeland Security by default, Health and Human Services for a biological incident, Agriculture for a drought) and its confirmed secretary, and the daily brief tells the president. Attacks and other national crises have no records yet; they join the list when an engine writes one.

whatItFakes: What the player prepares for a federal act (the stances a re-election filing runs on, the budget request's line changes, the joint address's answers) is kept in the federal day's own table, beside the engine's.
why: OFFICE-LOCAL's prepareAct takes only the local acts' ids; the federal day may not change the engine.
replacement: OFFICE-LOCAL's prepareAct taking any registered kit's act ids (asked on the PR); the federal table is deleted.

whatItFakes: Every state chamber and Congress keeps the same nine subject committees (finance, judiciary, education, health, labor and commerce, transportation, environment, housing, government), not its own list and names.
why: The audit found every bill going to one 'general' committee. Each chamber's own committee list is not in the data yet; the nine subjects are the ones nearly every chamber keeps.
replacement: Each chamber's standing committees and the subjects they hear, read from its rules (Book of the States Table 3.23 and each chamber's committee page), the way Congress's are in data/office-day/federal-committees.json.

whatItFakes: The civilian board costs the city a yearly amount per resident and is recorded against the police department, but no complaint against an officer is brought or reviewed.
why: No engine records a police-stop complaint, a board finding or officer discipline; the board's cost and its department are built.
replacement: GOV: the justice engine files a resident's complaint against an officer from a police stop and the board reviews it, its finding read by the department's discipline.

whatItFakes: Young adults are recorded as heard in juvenile court, but their cases still go to adult court.
why: Session A checked main: justice sentencing has no adult-versus-juvenile court-routing record. An age-labeled reach row cannot change a hearing or sentence. Re-checked Oct 15, 2026 against src/core2: still no engine records adult-versus-juvenile court routing; the justice engine hears only corruption cases.
replacement: GOV: the justice engine reads the juvenile age in force when it routes a defendant's case, and the sentence follows that court's range.
resolution: The engine routes each arrested person's case to juvenile or adult court by the juvenile age in force, and the sentence and cost follow that court (src/core2/public-safety.ts).

whatItFakes: A permit requirement is recorded on adults and the sheriff, but no one applies for, holds or is refused a permit.
why: Session A checked main: there is no carried-weapon or permit application record. Legal reach on an adult does not establish possession, an application or a permit decision. Re-checked Oct 15, 2026 against src/core2: still no engine records a carried weapon, a permit application or a permit decision.
replacement: GOV with OPUS-PEOPLE: the justice engine reads the permit law when a carried weapon is part of a case, and the sheriff's office issues permits.
resolution: Adults in gun-owning households apply for, hold and renew permits, paying the state fee and the class through the journal; adults under 21 are refused (src/core2/public-safety.ts).

whatItFakes: A purchase age is recorded on dealers and young adults, but no handgun sale is made or refused.
why: Session A checked main: purchases are aggregate money flows with no handgun sale or buyer-age check. Applying an age to every young adult would invent an attempted purchase. Re-checked Oct 15, 2026 against src/core2: still no engine records a handgun sale or a buyer-age check.
replacement: OPUS-WORLD: the business engine's sales read the purchase age when a store sells to a person.
resolution: Young adults in gun-owning households buy handguns from private sellers where no age limit applies and are refused where one does (src/core2/public-safety.ts).

whatItFakes: The rule is recorded on adults, but no self-defense case is charged or decided under it.
why: Session A checked main: justice has no self-defense incident or charging claim with retreat facts. A law row cannot establish those facts for an arbitrary defendant. Re-checked Oct 15, 2026 against src/core2: still no engine records a self-defense incident or a charging decision on one; the justice engine hears only corruption cases.
replacement: GOV: the prosecutor's charging decision and the court read the law in force when a case turns on self-defense.
resolution: Self-defense claims in assault cases end at charging where the rule is law, and only those with no safe retreat end there where the duty to retreat applies (src/core2/public-safety.ts).

whatItFakes: The ban is recorded on employers, landlords and residents, but no hiring or rental decision reads it and no complaint is brought.
why: Session A checked main: hiring and rental decisions have no protected-trait discrimination term or complaint record. Merely marking applicants protected would not change the decision. Re-checked Oct 15, 2026 against src/core2: still no engine records a protected trait in a hiring or rental decision, or a complaint about one.
replacement: OPUS-WORLD: hiring and renting read the ban when they weigh an applicant, and a refused applicant can bring a complaint the justice engine hears.

whatItFakes: The restriction is recorded on women of reproductive age and on providers, but no pregnancy is ever ended or carried because of it.
why: Session A checked main: renewal pregnancies come from agreed family plans; there is no unplanned pregnancy, termination request or provider decision to read the restriction. Re-checked Oct 15, 2026 against src/core2: still no engine records an unplanned pregnancy, a termination request or a provider decision.
replacement: OPUS-PEOPLE: the renewal engine models unplanned pregnancies and the woman's decision, reading the law in force where she lives, the distance to a provider and her own reasons.

whatItFakes: Parental consent is recorded on minors and on online businesses, but no account is opened, refused or verified.
why: Session A checked main: no minor account-opening, parental consent or verification service record exists. Applying an average compliance bill would not prove a minor was admitted or barred. Re-checked Oct 15, 2026 against src/core2: still no engine records a minor account, a parental consent or a verification service.
replacement: OPUS-PEOPLE: a teenager's media use and the parent's consent read the law; the online businesses' costs read the verification duty.

whatItFakes: The warrant rule is recorded on the police, but no investigation uses or is barred from facial recognition.
why: Session A checked main: justice investigations have witness, hearsay and payment evidence, but no facial-identification request or warrant record. Re-checked Oct 15, 2026 against src/core2: still no engine records a facial-identification request or warrant; the justice engine hears only corruption cases.
replacement: GOV: the justice engine's identification of a suspect reads the rule and needs a warrant where it applies.

whatItFakes: Rights are recorded on residents, but no request to see or delete data is made. The compliance cost is now read by the business engine (every employing business in town pays a share of its operating costs while the law is in force), but the law's coverage thresholds (revenue, number of consumers) are not modeled, so it falls on every employing business alike.
why: Session A checked main: no customer-data holdings or access/deletion request exists. The business engine's monthly cost review now reads the law (readDataPrivacyLaw in src/core2/modules/business.ts); what a request is, and which businesses hold enough data to be covered, have no records.
replacement: PEOPLE with WORLD: a resident's request to see or delete data, answered by a business that holds customer data; coverage thresholds from the statute's terms read per business.

whatItFakes: Broader local power is recorded on the town and its council, but the authority check still reads only the specific grants.
why: Session A checked main: legislature.authorityFor returns specific wage/tax grants and policy preemptions; otherwise it already permits local policy questions. There is no undecided authority category whose permission a broader grant would change. A read returning the same result would not prove an effect.
replacement: GOV: authorityFor reads home rule in force as a grant for any question the state hasn't decided.
resolvedBy: Claude (laws-record-only-reads), Oct 15: policyAuthority (src/core2/policy-authority.ts) already reads the state's home-rule law for every question the powers catalog leaves open for a city; it was proven only by a hand-inserted fixture. src/core2/home-rule-played.test.ts now shows, in a generated town, a council's draft of such an ordinance blocked with the grant repealed, drafted once the state's grant takes effect (the bill's authority row cites the grant's law id), and blocked again on repeal.

whatItFakes: The player's household is evicted like any other when its rent goes unpaid: notice, filing, hearing, judgment and removal under the place's law.
why: Whether the player can lose their home is the owner's call (homelessness package, Oct 14); the package's default is yes.
replacement: The owner's ruling: keep it as is, or give the player's household another path.
resolution: docs/coordination/OWNER-DECISIONS.md, 'Homelessness is a factor' (Oct 14): 'A person who does not work and does not pay loses their home like anyone else; the player's household too.' Same notice, filing, hearing and judgment as anyone (docs/packages/homelessness.md).

whatItFakes: A place's shelter beds are its state's year-round beds per 10,000 people (HUD 2025 Housing Inventory Count) times its own people, not the beds its Continuum of Care actually lists in or near it.
why: The HIC lists beds by Continuum of Care and provider; joining providers' geocodes to places is not done yet.
replacement: Beds by place from the HIC provider rows (geocode to county and place), with occupancy on the count night.

whatItFakes: American Samoa and the Northern Mariana Islands, which have no HUD Continuum of Care, use the nation's shelter beds per 10,000.
why: No HUD Housing Inventory Count covers them.
replacement: Each territory government's own shelter count.

whatItFakes: A state's foreclosure timeline that was not read from its statute (or that has no published average) is taken from secondary summaries or the national average days to complete.
why: Foreclosure statutes and timelines were gathered for 56 places in one pass; places below high confidence still need their statute text read.
replacement: Each place's foreclosure steps read from its statute text and court rules, with its own average days to complete.

whatItFakes: The desktop shell's update dialogs (Check for Updates, and the Mac note on what installing does) are written in the shell, not by the English engine.
why: The shell runs outside the game, where the English engine is not loaded; the owner ordered a plain dialog telling the player what the Mac install does (Oct 14, 2026).
replacement: Shell lines drawn from an English-engine bank shipped beside the client, read by main.mjs.

whatItFakes: The Windows package job (and the Windows build in each release) may fail without failing the checks or blocking the Mac release.
why: Owner's call (Oct 14, 2026): the Mac build is what matters now; Windows can stay red until early access.
replacement: Early-access preparation: the Windows job made green and required again, and every release carrying latest.yml.
resolution: docs/coordination/OWNER-DECISIONS.md: 'The Mac package is the one that must pass; the Windows row stays allowed-to-fail until early access.' docs/coordination/BOARD.md: 'Windows may stay red until early access.' The workflow keeps continue-on-error on the Windows row on that ruling.

whatItFakes: New game writes the chosen name, birth date, gender and appearance recipe straight onto the new world's player record from the play handler, instead of through a core API.
why: The new core has no API for setting the player's identity after a world is built; the old creator lived on the retired engine.
replacement: An OPUS-CORE identity call (name, birth date, sex, appearance) that the creator uses and that keeps indexes and records consistent. Resolved Oct 16, 2026: CoreAPI.chooseIdentityV1 (controlled player only, before the first day passes) is what the creator calls; the bench no longer writes person fields.

whatItFakes: Changing the age in the creator moves only the birth date; the life's generated past (schooling, work, household, family ages) stays as it was drawn for the original age.
why: World building draws the player's past during New game, before the creator runs, and there is no step to redraw it for a chosen age.
replacement: New game passes the chosen age and birthday into the world build (or a core redraw of the player's past) so the history matches the age.

whatItFakes: A member with no person record (a seat held by no one filled in) is present at every vote; every other member decides from their own day.
why: The audit found nobody ever absent. A member without a person record has no day, health or temperament to miss a vote from.
replacement: Every seat's holder filled in as a person before they vote, so attendance reads their day like anyone's. Done Oct 16: a seat whose holder has no living person record casts no vote and moves no pill, so the stand-in is gone.

whatItFakes: A member with no person record never moves a poison pill; every other member decides from their own temperament.
why: A member without a person record has no traits for the chooser to read.
replacement: Every seat's holder filled in as a person before they vote, so floor tactics read their temperament like anyone's. Done Oct 16: a seat whose holder has no living person record casts no vote and moves no pill, so the stand-in is gone.

whatItFakes: A job offer's deadline stops the player's clock once as a reminder instead of holding it until the player answers; an unanswered offer lapses as the employer's withdrawal.
why: The play screen has no control yet to answer a job offer; a held deadline would stop the clock for good.
replacement: A held offer-deadline stop once the play screen shows jobOffersFor with accept and decline controls (OPUS-PLAY).

whatItFakes: Completed rentals match local rent-saving tenants, recovered homeless households, and unassigned households in either tier. Job-location and family-space matching are not modeled.
why: Rent, income and cash are read; dwelling capacity and commute preferences still lack records.
replacement: Read recorded job locations and dwelling capacity to weigh commute and family-space changes with the same decision rule in both tiers.

whatItFakes: A municipal collective in a town whose government the game has not compiled is named after the town and "Council"; a compiled town's body takes the name its charter gives it.
why: Only the 144 compiled municipal governments carry a charter reading; every other town's charter is unread. Narrowed Oct 19: the compiled readers now carry the body name.
replacement: Carry each charter’s collective body name into the municipal reading and replace the default.

whatItFakes: Until jurisdiction-specific dual-office exceptions are compiled, the data conservatively treats two elected mandates as incompatible. The federal legislative/executive prohibition is sourced separately.
why: The repository has no per-place dual-office compilation; the previous engine vacated every prior office without reading any law. Research endpoint returned a web application firewall block.
replacement: Source each place’s prohibitions and exceptions, replacing the estimated pairs in the same reader.

whatItFakes: A question with no mapping in the powers catalog, or a local question whose gating state law is not on record, cannot be introduced; the authority result records a disputed missing grant rather than silently permitting the action. (Oct 15: a territory's cell the catalog has not read now takes its state cell, an estimate; see SG-GOV-policy-power-conditions.)
why: All 59 policy questions are mapped. What remains unresolved is a gating state law not yet recorded, which the engine cannot infer from absent research.
replacement: The gating state laws recorded in the opening law table for every place, read before introduction and executive orders.

whatItFakes: Inherited game-profile powers cells are provisional estimates; a cell explicitly marked limited retains a disputed grant while its qualitative conditions are not yet all executable predicates. A territory's unread cell is its state cell (data/research/powers-catalog/territory-grant.json), an estimate.
why: The shared research catalog includes unsourced game-profile cells and records some conditional powers in prose rather than structured constraints.
replacement: Sourced per-place cells and structured conditions for each limited power, evaluated by the same authority reader before introduction or an executive order.

whatItFakes: Background Congress uses the shared platform question pool, which lacks most federal-only questions in the powers catalog. Only supported questions with federal scope can be proposed; state-specific questions no longer stand in for federal policy.
why: Federal-only policy questions need recorded starting answers, official stances and downstream effect readers before adding them to the shared proposal pool.
replacement: Wire the federal-only questions through the existing stance, law and effect engines, with named-person played-world evidence, then include them in the proposal pool.

whatItFakes: The state officeholder's day runs on this file's own small module: tomorrow's entries are scheduled the evening before, and any the player has not done by the morning, a stop included, the character does on its own (a stop that lapses is marked so).
why: OFFICE-LOCAL's office-day engine (src/core2/modules/office-day.ts), which pauses the clock on a stop, is not on main yet; the package says build against the smallest stand-in meanwhile. Replaced by the shared office-day engine and its desk in Session C.
replacement: The office-day engine's calendar, stop and simulate-or-do loop, with the state's entries and acts from this file as its rows.

whatItFakes: District office hours decide only the cases already open for the state legislator, and the constituent-cases engine routes residents' problems to council members and the mayor only, so a state legislator's office receives none.
why: Routing is the constituent-cases engine's (OPUS-GOV); forking it here would make a second engine. Session C routes cases through the sitting local and state district terms covering the town.
replacement: The constituent-cases engine routes a resident's problem to the state legislator whose district covers them as well as to local officials, by the same choice of whom they know best.

whatItFakes: Item vetoes now strike or reduce appropriation increases and use exact override fractions and joint totals. Special deadlines, external assent, and some protected or mixed appropriation categories remain incomplete.
why: Session C wires surviving amounts into budget enactment. Imported legal details remain estimated; unsupported territorial reductions are unavailable, and mixed administration appropriations are blocked where protected branch spending cannot be separated. The played year now proves struck and reduced increases reaching the adopted budget, treasury providers and named owners. The owners’ learned attribution and director scene remain unproved.
replacement: An item veto in the legislature engine: the executive strikes (or reduces, where the data allows) budget lines, each item goes back for its override vote at the data's share, and the budgets engine adopts what stands.

whatItFakes: A bill on the player's desk that the character decides on its own is signed when the character's position plus their traits' lean toward signing is not negative; the legislature engine's own rule for any other executive also weighs how settled the law is.
why: That rule is internal to the legislature engine (OPUS-GOV); this file reads only what it exports. Replaced by the shared office-day engine and its desk in Session C.
replacement: The legislature engine exports the executive's own choice on a bill, used for the player's character as for any executive.

whatItFakes: Dev mode's custom start as a sitting state officeholder ends the seat's serving term and writes the player's term into the offices engine's table directly, keeping the previous holder's party; it is not reached in ordinary play.
why: The offices engine has no exported way to seat a chosen person (its own seatResident is internal); the package's proof and the owner's play need a custom start today.
replacement: An offices-engine function to seat a chosen person for the rest of a term (OPUS-GOV), with the player's own party from the parties engine, called by dev mode.

whatItFakes: Savings and withdrawals are reviewed monthly with a three-month wallet reserve; extraordinary payments and estate settlement do not yet request bank withdrawals directly. Dormant claims remain owed, not deleted.
why: The existing payment paths consume cash directly. A bounded monthly policy allows deposits to fund lending without duplicating cash or claiming all payments are deposit-aware.
replacement: Have payment and estate writers withdraw from the same named deposit claim before declaring a cash shortfall; preserve household claims across family changes.

whatItFakes: The bank holds opening mortgages whose original funding is an unmatched opening liability, not named customer deposits. New savings deposits are actual journal transfers and are accounted for separately.
why: The pre-existing mortgage opening subtracts its initial principal from capital without recording who funded it. Retaining that offset avoids creating capital or cash while adding new deposits.
replacement: Generate the mortgage opening with named depositor or warehouse-funding liabilities and retain those funding records in the bank books.

whatItFakes: Repealing a starting graduated income-tax schedule uses the existing estimated state or local flat rate. The binary catalog provision carries no replacement rate, deduction or filing-status rules.
why: Tax Foundation's 2025 state survey and actual conversion laws have distinct enacted rates and deductions. The catalog's Boolean question cannot supply those terms. Received explanation and director acceptance remain unproven.
replacement: Explicit replacement tax terms in the provision, read by the existing withholding engine for full and counted workers, with a received explanation and director line for an affected worker.

whatItFakes: No town income-growth observation or local feedback is available before enough comparable paid-income months exist; the national economy continues from its national records.
why: The played world records paid town income only from opening and does not have comparable pre-start income receipts.
replacement: Pre-start town paid-income records produced from the opening economy, so year-over-year feedback can be computed from real records immediately.
resolution: Done Oct 16 (world-stopgap-macro-missing-record): the national step hears the nation's payroll-income growth over the same twelve months as the estimate of the town's growth (townGrowthEstimatePct on each simulated month), and the town's own paid-income growth takes over by a twelfth of the weight for each comparable month it covers (townGrowthOwnWeight). No month omits local feedback.

whatItFakes: A known counted relative can receive a death notice, but opening full-to-counted family ties lack recorded closeness; grief is supported only where a relationship record already exists. No closeness is invented by the notifier.
why: The core opening skips relationship initialization when the other person is a husk. The bench also retains the full family closure; the drawn Garden City year had zero known counted deaths, so the notification path has no played-year acceptance yet.
replacement: Initialize full-to-counted family relationship records through the shared core rule and reconcile the bench with the core opening; then prove a native counted death, notice and reaction in the same drawn played world.

whatItFakes: A council seat chosen by part of town counts only the voters of its part: the town's households in their recorded order are cut into equal runs, one per seat chosen that way, and the counted residents and the rest of the town divide equally among them. No part of town has a boundary or a street behind it.
why: The world holds no street map or address inside a town, and no record of how a place's council districts or wards are drawn.
replacement: Council districts drawn from the town's dwellings (by the council or a commission, to near equal population as its charter says), each household and each sitting member placed by their dwelling.

whatItFakes: A state or national party's officers in the standing pool: only the town's local party chair is recorded, so the pool's party officers are the chairs of the state's parties as the town sees them.
why: The parties engine records one local committee and its chair per party, not a state committee, its officers or a national committee.
replacement: The parties engine records state and national committees and their officers; the pool reads them in place of the local chair.

whatItFakes: Where a place has no researched failure-to-elect row for an office family, the holdover rule is the family estimate (data/offices/holdover.json). Repeat special elections are dated by the state's special-election rule or its estimate. National presidential failure-to-elect is not implemented.
why: Existing vacancy data governs filling a vacancy but does not establish when failure to elect creates one. Only congressional fixed term boundaries are sourced here.
replacement: A researched failure-to-elect row for each of the 56 places and each office family, and the national presidential contingent-election path.

whatItFakes: Wider races reach named officials across their jurisdiction and the played town residents. Unnamed ordinary residents elsewhere have no candidate records. State legislative district residency is not individually known for officials stored at state scope.
why: The wider electorate has counts but no resident household records from which candidacy can read personal resources and ambitions.
replacement: Jurisdiction-wide counted household records with district membership, using the same candidacy reasons before filling in a runner.

whatItFakes: Uses the CTO ruling that working press staff and outlet owners cannot run for office while retaining that role.
why: OWNER-DECISIONS.md records the October 14, 2026 ruling as pending owner confirmation.
replacement: Owner confirmation or revision of the press-employment conflict rule; apply the chosen rule to all candidate filing paths.
resolution: Done Oct 19 (gov-press-ban-withdrawn): the owner withdrew the ban on Oct 16 ("a reporter who wants to run may run"; OWNER-DECISIONS). The press-employment check is gone from checkEligibility, the candidacy chooser and the candidate pool, so press staff file and run like anyone; only the automatic vacancy stand-in still passes over press jobs, because the defect was a reporter seated without an election.

whatItFakes: The state-chamber party-loyalty weight (weights.statePartyLoyalty, 1) is checked against the federal party-unity figure (about 0.90, CQ Vote Studies) because the state roll-call calibration input is not in the repository.
why: The owner ruled on Oct 15 that his own state roll-call input may calibrate this one parameter, with nothing from it shipped or cited; a builder session does not hold that input.
replacement: Run the owner's state roll-call input against the simulated chambers (src/core2/party-loyalty.test.ts measures them), set statePartyLoyalty and the test's target from it, and close this row.

whatItFakes: A central bank candidate's place on the left-right scale is read from how much inflation they lived through against the board (more is a hawk, on the Republican side), so the president's party picks the candidates nearest their own side.
why: Presidents of either party have named hawks and doves; no source ties a nominee's lived inflation to a party, so this is an assumed link.
replacement: A nominee's party or stated views as a record on the candidate, read for alignment; or a sourced relation between appointing party and hawkishness.

whatItFakes: How qualified a candidate's career makes them is a small table by career, not read from the candidate's record of work.
why: A seeded candidate has a career label and a lived-inflation figure, and no work history to weigh.
replacement: Qualification read from the candidate's recorded career history, with the table's values calibrated to the careers of past governors.

whatItFakes: A contest filed with a state or territory election board, commission or division (not the secretary of state) names no clerk: the filing scene shows the office's title with no one at the counter.
why: The state election agencies are titles in the filing data; no record lists their staff, and a board has no single holder to name.
replacement: Resolved Oct 16: the executive engine seats a chief election official for the state (appointment post chief-election-official), a full person on the state payroll, and the filing clerk returns them (pool item gov-state-election-office-holder).

whatItFakes: The federal government pays its officials (the president, vice president, senators and representatives), and another state's government pays its own, as an outside party recorded on the journal, and receives what escheats to it; their pay is paid in full while the taxes withheld from it go to every treasury the world keeps.
why: The town's federal treasury holds only the town's share of federal taxes (a few hundred thousand dollars a month), too little to pay a national payroll, and no other state keeps a treasury here. Paid from the federal treasury, the president's pay came out at about $500 in a month.
replacement: A federal treasury at national scale and a coarse treasury for every other state, so their officials are paid from them and their estates settle to them.

whatItFakes: Guam, American Samoa, the Northern Marianas and the U.S. Virgin Islands have no legislative-district geography or member roster in the data, so each chamber's recorded seats are all elected at large by the whole territory.
why: The Census Gazetteer legislative districts cover the states, D.C. and Puerto Rico only; the territories' own districts (Guam at large, the Virgin Islands by island, the Northern Marianas by island and village, American Samoa's counties and districts) are not yet read.
replacement: Each territory's districts and sitting members, read from the territory's election commission, so seats are elected by district and hold the real parties and names.

whatItFakes: A body with committees takes a scheduled bill to its committee a week ahead of the floor, and the committee decides on its own day without the pre-vote hooks that run on the floor day: staff briefings, interest groups organizing, public comment and the player's own vote. Whether any of them belong to the committee day (a public comment at the committee's hearing, a briefing before a committee vote) is the owner's call.
why: Moving the committee off the floor day split it from the hooks that run just before a vote. The simplest version keeps every hook on the floor day, as before, so nothing already built changes order.
replacement: The owner's ruling on which pre-vote hooks run on the committee day (docs/coordination/OWNER-DECISIONS.md).

whatItFakes: In a state where a board, council or senate holds or must concur in clemency (board alone, board with the governor, governor with a board's recommendation, a council's or the senate's consent), the governor's day has no clemency act: the board's own decisions are not simulated, so no prisoner is released there by clemency.
why: The governor decides alone only where the state's law says so (governor alone, or a board that only advises); the other authorities need a board or council engine that does not exist yet.
replacement: A clemency board engine (members, petitions, recommendations) and the council or senate consent, read by the governor's act where the law requires it.

whatItFakes: A town's police, fire, public works and public health departments and its local government offices are paid by the town's own government (its city or village, else its township), a state office in town by its state and a post office by the nation. The opening's data does not say which unit employs a given department, so the link is assumed.
why: The departments held no cash and no pay link, so their workers were never paid. The Census of Governments lists functions by government but not which unit staffs a town's own departments.
replacement: Each department's employing government read from the Census of Governments employment file by function, so a county health department, a fire district or a state agency's field office pays its own staff.

whatItFakes: Two housing links move nothing: air-conditioning use does not rise or fall with the electricity price, and the share of income a place's renters pay in rent does not change how many people are homeless.
why: The cited research gives no usable size: the electricity-price link has no published slope and no engine reads the air-conditioning share; the rent-burden link has thresholds at 22 and 32 percent but no slope (Zillow and UNH 2018; Colburn and Aldern 2022).
replacement: A sized link (a published slope per point of burden or per cent of price) read by an engine that decides air-conditioning use and by the homeless review.

whatItFakes: A severe disaster does not lower home values: the link needs the disaster's death toll and the disasters module records only the FEMA declaration and its payments.
why: Boustan, Kahn, Rhode and Yanguas 2020 size the price effect for disasters with at least 20 deaths; no record of deaths per disaster exists, and home values are not a factor the sales engine reads.
replacement: Deaths and damage recorded on each disaster by the disasters module, and the housing sales engine reading the web's home-price factor.

whatItFakes: Full couples decide on a child from their own age, children, work, income, room, savings, health and closeness, and none of the outcome web's birth links reach them. Counted women take the web's factor per woman (src/core2/births-counted.ts), so a full woman and a counted woman of the same age, tenure and place differ on the links the full decision does not carry: home prices (owners up, renters down), an enforced abortion ban, and the place's drifting birth level.
why: The unemployment link is left out for full couples on purpose: a lost job already lowers their work and income terms, so the web's link would count the same recession twice. The other links have no term in the plan score, and the score is a choice between planning and waiting, not a rate the factor can multiply; turning a factor into a score term needs its own calibration against the births it produces.
replacement: A conditions term in the plan score that reads webReach for the woman's own age and tenure, leaving out the links her own records already carry (unemployment), with a weight calibrated in a played year so full births move by the researched size, as counted births do.

whatItFakes: Conscientiousness shifts who falls seriously ill and who holds behavior-driven conditions for full people only; a counted group draws its illnesses and deaths from the life-table share without its members' traits.
why: The counted flows (renewal) pick who is ill by the group's share, and a group has no per-member hazard to scale; the factor is rescaled to the opening mean so totals still match the life tables, but the group's own trait mix does not move its rate.
replacement: Counted illness reads the group's mean of the same factor (exp of the slope times each member's level, from the packed trait columns) when a month's owed illnesses are booked; a person filled in from a group already carries their own.

whatItFakes: Counted people's trait columns do not move with age or life events while they are counted; they are brought to their age norm in one step when filled in.
why: Their traits are read in place from one packed column per group, shared by the lean cache; changing them each birthday would need a per-member cache drop for every counted person.
replacement: Groups apply the same yearly shift to their columns by age band once the counted store can drop a member's cached lean.

whatItFakes: 27 laws (listed in outcome-research-gaps.json, each with the outcome its research would measure) move no outcome-web measure: no researched link starts from the law or from a measure an engine sets from it, so the web holds those outcomes at their base whatever the law does.
why: data/research/outcome-web/links.json has no link from these laws or their measures; the laws' reach, engine reads and money are wired, but an outcome link needs a researched strength, shape and lag before the web can move anything.
replacement: A researched link per law in links.json (strength, shape, lag, source), built by the outcome-web line, after which each row leaves outcome-research-gaps.json.

whatItFakes: The web's uninsured-share links (unemployment, Medicaid expansion, the work requirement, marriage equality) and the Medicaid medical-debt link move the web's own health.uninsured-pct number; no person's or counted household's coverage decision reads the factor.
why: The coverage record (modules/coverage.ts, counted households included) is on branch claude/coverage-counted (PR 5475) and not on main; the coverage code belongs to another session.
replacement: Once the coverage record is on main, the coverage decision reads webFactorFor("health.uninsured-pct", subject) with the moderators already in links.json (unemployment by sex and age), and medical debt reads the coverage record.

whatItFakes: Deaths carry no cause. The traffic link moves the share of deaths a crash stands for at each age (IIHS rate over the life table's death rate), not a crash-death record. The overdose links (harm reduction, cannabis sales) and the youth firearm links (child access law, minimum handgun age) move only the web's number; no death reads them.
why: Overdose and firearm death rates by single age are not in the repo, and a death has no cause field (death-causes.ts holds three plain groups).
replacement: A cause-of-death record on every death, with cause-specific hazards by age (crash, overdose, firearm) from CDC WONDER, read by the people engines; the web's factor then multiplies each cause's hazard.

whatItFakes: Child asthma, teen cannabis use and Medicare out-of-pocket drug cost (gas hookup ban, cannabis sales, drug price negotiation) move only the web's number.
why: No condition, use or prescription record exists for a child's asthma, a teen's cannabis use or an enrollee's drug spending; condition-pack.ts holds adult chronic conditions only.
replacement: A childhood asthma condition, a teen substance-use record and Part D spending on the household's books, each decided from the engine's own records times the web's factor.

whatItFakes: Congestion to premature births, heat to deaths, education to mortality and eviction to hospital visits have no researched size, so nothing moves.
why: The links are unsized in links.json and no producer exists for premature births, heat deaths or hospital visits.
replacement: Sized links from fetched research, then the death and birth engines read them like the wired ones.

whatItFakes: Coverage to catastrophic bills, medical debt, depression and mortality; job loss to death risk; long hours to heart disease; childhood food stamps to adult health; the earned income credit to low birth weight are person-level links with no cause recorded on the person.
why: A person's coverage history, displacement, weekly hours, childhood benefit years and a birth weight are not stored.
replacement: Records on the person for each cause, read by the health engine's hazard like the web's death factor.

whatItFakes: The town hears of a rise in housing.rent from the outcome web's month record, but no engine yet reads the web's rent factor when it sets a lease, so the rise the story reports is not in any lease or rent payment.
why: The housing family's rent wiring is on its own branch; the news path lists the measure so the town hears of it the month an engine reads it, with no change here.
replacement: The housing engine multiplies its lease rent by webFactorFor(housing.rent); then this row and the readBy null in data/news/outcome-news.json are replaced by the reading file.

whatItFakes: The web's youth firearm death and suicide rates become an expected count of young people lost in the town each month, but no named child dies of it.
why: Counted people die only through the illness-course engine (births-counted.ts); there is no injury death for a child.
replacement: PEOPLE: an injury death for full and counted young people, booked from this expected count.

whatItFakes: The immigration partnership moves the web's Hispanic school enrollment, undocumented employment and U.S.-born employment, but no school or jobs engine reads those measures.
why: The detainer holds are built; the three outcomes are kept place measures that no engine consumes.
replacement: WORLD and PEOPLE: school enrollment and jobs engines read the kept measures when they enroll and hire.

whatItFakes: The named residents' share of ordinary-crime arrests is carried in an unnamed batch of cases; no named person is arrested, held or sentenced by this engine.
why: A named person is charged only through an act the engines record (corruption cases today); there is no engine that records an ordinary offense as a named person's own act.
replacement: PEOPLE and GOV: an act engine where a named person's drives, record and circumstances decide an offense, then the case flow charges them from that act.

whatItFakes: Couples exist only as the opening drew them: no one partners, marries, separates or divorces during play, so the temperament reads that should decide those (extraversion raises the odds of a first marriage 1.35 per standard deviation and openness lowers them 0.77, Jokela et al. 2011; neuroticism raises divorce r = 0.17, agreeableness lowers it r = -0.18, Roberts et al. 2007) have no decision to read them.
why: The partnership engine is gated in the pool (people-partnerships-full-people-form and people-partnerships-full-people-end wait on core family-link and household-membership changes). The effect sizes are in data/research/trait-effect-sizes.json (outcome.marriage-formation, outcome.divorce).
replacement: When partnerships form and end in play, the forming and ending decisions read both partners' traits through leanedYes with weights calibrated from those rows by scripts/traits/trait-calibrate.ts.

whatItFakes: A full person's leaving does not weigh the state income tax in force: only counted households do (counted-moves.ts reads the town state's income-tax law and the other states' 2026 table into an income pull). The web's income-tax links are about zero (Young, Varner, Lurie and Prisinzano 2016), so they add nothing on top, and adding them would count the tax twice for counted households.
why: A full person's destination is chosen after the pull is built, so a tax difference between states has no place to enter the pull until a destination-aware pull exists.
replacement: A destination-aware pull for full people that uses the same net-of-tax income comparison as pullBetween in counted-moves.ts.

whatItFakes: The link from a severe disaster to out-migration (Boustan, Kahn, Rhode and Yanguas 2020) does not run: no record says how many people a disaster killed in a place. The disasters engine holds FEMA declarations (type, begin and declared dates) with no deaths, and the research's effect starts at about 100 deaths.
why: A declaration is not a severity; reading one as severe would move every declared place by a guess.
replacement: A per-place count of deaths from a disaster (the health engine's cause-of-death records within the incident's dates) read as the link's cause disaster.severe.

whatItFakes: A public work (a capital line awarded to a town firm for the fiscal year) is finished on the day the next fiscal year's budget takes over, whatever was built. The treasury's payments to the contractor are real; the finish date is the year's end, not a completion the work reached.
why: The treasury pays the awarded firm by the month and nothing tracks the work itself: there is no schedule, milestone or completion record for a road, park, housing or school work.
replacement: A project record with a start, a cost, milestones the contractor's payments fund and a completion date the funded work reaches, which the office day reads for the ribbon.

whatItFakes: Only full people hold a health coverage record and pay a premium. Counted households hold none, so the wider population pays no premium and the town's health costs read as if it were uninsured.
why: The counted groups store holds no per-group plan, and a counted premium is a purchase flow with an insurer payee that fill-in must take back contract by contract (opening-customers.ts, residents.ts).
replacement: A coverage share per counted group, read by the same rule as a full person times the group's weight, and a premium flow per covered counted household (pool item people-coverage-counted).

whatItFakes: Press enrolls its already recorded owner directly in the business owner table because the shared business module has no public enrollment function for an existing owner.
why: The overnight order requires the smallest registered stand-in while the business interface is under active work; using the normal opening heuristic would incorrectly make a reporter the owner.
replacement: A shared business enrollment API accepting the existing owner and sourced books, used by press without direct table writes.

whatItFakes: Posted bail goes into the prosecuting government's general treasury cash, so the treasury can spend it before the trial and hand back only what it still holds; the shortfall is recorded on the return, not escrowed.
why: The journal has no court fund or escrow account to set bail aside; adding one is a new account kind under the treasury's owner.
replacement: A court escrow fund account that holds each bail apart from spendable treasury cash, returned in full at disposition.
